title: Molecular predictors of minimal residual disease in newly diagnosed multiple myeloma treated with quadruplet therapy
desc: Quadruplet therapy, combining anti-CD38 antibodies, immunomodulatory drugs, proteasome inhibitors and dexamethasone, is now the standard induction treatment for newly diagnosed multiple myeloma (NDMM). However, treatment response is heterogeneous and molecular predictors are needed to guide early therapeutic decisions. We performed integrated genomic, transcriptomic and epigenomic profiling of 423 tumor samples from patients with NDMM from the MIDAS cohort to characterize molecular heterogeneity and its association with measurable residual disease (MRD) after quadruplet induction with isatuximab, carfilzomib, lenalidomide and dexamethasone (Isa-KRd). Postinduction MRD-negativity rates varied significantly across gene expression subtypes, with HP1/HP3 and MS groups showing superior responses compared to the MF and CD2 subtypes. B cell differentiation was associated with MRD positivity, while proliferation and MYC programs were associated with MRD negativity. These MRD-associated transcriptomic features were independently validated in the CASSIOPEIA cohort. Whole-genome sequencing revealed both known (APOBEC mutagenesis, chromothripsis) and new genomic instability phenotypes validated in the MMRF cohort. New driver alterations were identified with independent validation across three external cohorts with multiple myeloma (MMRF, MANHATTAN and CASSIOPEIA; 1,451 cases). Genomic instability features and driver genes such as CCND1 and MYC correlated with differential MRD outcomes. DNA methylation profiling identified nine MRD-linked subgroups distinguished by the extent of hypomethylation in quiescent chromatin and cis / trans signatures of driver translocations. A multimodal random forest model integrating genomic, transcriptomic and epigenomic features predicted MRD status after induction, with an area under the curve of 0.77, outperforming clinical and genomic models, while providing comparable discrimination and improved calibration relative to the transcriptomic and epigenomic models. title: Variability in automated sepsis case detection: a systematic analysis of implementation methods in clinical data repositories.
source: PubMed · Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
desc: [Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA] To systematically review and characterize methodological heterogeneity in sepsis case detection using the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care III (MIMIC-III) and eICU-CRD databases. We conducted a PRISMA-guided systematic review of PubMed and Web of Science (publication years 2016-2024). Studies were eligible if they applied the SOFA-based Sepsis-3 definition to MIMIC-III or eICU-CRD, provided at least one explicit label-calculation detail, reported a traceable detection rate, and met further criteria detailed in the PRISMA flow diagram. We classified each study by study type and unit of analysis (patients, admissions, or ICU stays) and extracted methodological details on sepsis case detection across 6 domains. For studies with available source code, we additionally examined code structure and repository dependencies to identify methodological decisions across these domains. Of 396 publications screened, 64 met inclusion criteria and 12 provided source code. Sepsis detection rates ranged from 3.4% to 65.2% in MIMIC-III and from 9.8% to 47.9% in eICU-CRD. Substantial variability persisted among studies using identical cohort definitions within both databases (MIMIC-III: 16.9%-42.2%; eICU-CRD: 13.9%-31.4%). In a generalized linear mixed model, between-study heterogeneity was extreme (overall τ²≈0.79; 95% prediction interval for a new study's detection rate 5%-63%), and study-level characteristics-including database, study type, infection detection method, code availability, and unit of analysis-explained only a small proportion of this variance (≈9%), with no characteristic reaching statistical significance. The overall proportion of studies reporting methodological details varied by domain: SOFA calculation (53.1%), infection detection methods (42.2%), temporal windows (37.5%), aggregation methods (26.6%), and missing-data handling (17.2%). Source code analysis identified 321 implementation decisions, revealing heterogeneity in baseline SOFA definitions (SOFA = 0 vs dynamic baseline), temporal windows (infection-centered vs ICU-admission-centered) and infection detection methods (antibiotic-culture matching vs APACHE-based diagnosis). Dependencies among several MIMIC-III repositories suggested propagation of implementation decisions across studies. title: Expertise modulates automation bias and sentinel behavior in human–AI collaborative diagnosis of neonatal pneumoperitoneum
desc: Medical AI is often validated under an additive assumption that algorithmic sensitivity and clinician oversight will combine to improve care. We tested this assumption in the high-stakes diagnosis of neonatal pneumoperitoneum, a time-critical surgical emergency. In a multi-reader crossover study analyzing 1750 interpretation events, clinicians reviewed radiographs aided by either a high-reliability model or a systematically error-injected model. We found that high AI reliability paradoxically induces automation bias in trainees, who accepted 52.0% of incorrect suggestions, while offering limited gains to experts. Conversely, when challenged by flawed AI, the three participating neonatologists exhibited a “sentinel behavior” phenotype, correctly overriding 91.7% of errors (Wilson 95% CI: 83.0–96.0%) consistent with increased deliberation; given the small specialist cohort, this finding is hypothesis-generating and warrants prospective replication. We operationalize systemic resilience as the capacity to maintain diagnostic integrity under algorithmic failure and demonstrate that clinical validity depends on the human–AI team’s adversarial resilience rather than standalone accuracy. To mitigate the risk of deskilling and never-skilling, we release an open-source educational sandbox designed to inoculate clinicians against automated errors.

title: The Current Status and Evaluation of Artificial Intelligence in Bladder Cancer: Clinical Applications and Research.
source: PubMed · Computational and structural biotechnology journal
desc: [Computational and structural biotechnology journal] Bladder cancer ranks as the 10th most common malignancy worldwide. Advances in technology are continuously reshaping its diagnosis, treatment selection, and prognosis assessment. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has demonstrated marked potential in transforming bladder cancer care. By integrating and analyzing multi-source data, AI enhances the precision and efficiency of disease management. This review comprehensively examines the current applications of AI across various domains, including radiographic imaging analysis, pathological diagnosis, cystoscopic image processing, molecular subtyping, drug development, organoid research, prognostic modeling, and medical device innovation. It highlights the advantages of AI over conventional methods, outlines model development strategies, and summarizes commonly employed algorithms. Furthermore, we discuss the key challenges in translating AI tools into real-world clinical practice. This narrative review aims to inform the future development of AI-driven digital health systems, ultimately contributing to the realization of precision medicine and personalized management for bladder cancer patients.

The program uses artificial intelligence (AI). It sorts tumours into three groups: * benign: not cancer * borderline: abnormal cells that usually behave less aggressively than cancer * malignant: cancer Before surgery, doctors try to judge which group a tumour belongs to. This guides where and how the operation is done. This judgement is often hard, especially for borderline tumours. An AI program that does it well could help doctors plan surgery. The main questions it aims to answer are: * How well does the AI program sort ovarian tumours into benign, borderline and malignant on CT scans? * Does the AI program work as well on scans from hospitals it did not learn from? Researchers will compare the AI program's results with the final diagnosis from the tumour tissue removed during surgery. They will also compare the program with methods doctors use today, such as ultrasound-based risk scores and the radiologist's report. In a smaller group, researchers will test the program on MRI scans. This study only uses information that already exists. It includes adults who had surgery for a mass in or near the ovary at hospitals in the Netherlands and Belgium. Researchers will use: * CT or MRI scans made before surgery as part of regular care * information from medical records * the tissue diagnosis after surgery Participants will not be contacted. They will not have any extra scans, tests or visits. Each hospital codes the data before sharing them, so researchers cannot see participants' names. The study does not change anyone's care.

title: Heterogeneous Agentic Coevolution
desc: Recent advances in self-improving LLM agents have demonstrated the potential of AI systems that drive their own intelligence. However, many domain-specific applications rely on specialized foundation models that possess strong domain expertise but remain dependent on human-designed improvements. Extending recursive self-improvement to these models presents a key challenge: as a specialist improves, the strategies used to advance it must also adapt. To address this challenge, we propose Heterogeneous Agentic CoEvolution (HACE), a framework that jointly evolves specialized foundation models and LLM agents through reciprocal learning. HACE improves the specialist through supervised learning while training the agent with on-policy reinforced self-training, guided by verified performance gains on the current specialist. The agent's exploration, in turn, informs subsequent specialist training, enabling both models to adapt to each other's progress. To sustain this reciprocal learning, HACE further employs evolutionary search to optimize their interaction harness, adapting how the models exchange information and select training experiences as their capabilities evolve. We evaluate HACE across three challenging domains: recommendation systems, protein function prediction in biology, and crystal stability prediction in material discovery. We show that HACE outperforms the evaluated self-improving methods on the primary task metrics across all three domains. These results shed light on heterogeneous coevolution as a universal approach to improving specialized foundation models through reciprocal interaction with a learning agent.

title: A general-purpose System One decision model for clinical records
desc: Clinical care, health-system operations and biomedical discovery depend on extracting reliable answers from patient records, yet applying diverse clinical questions across entire populations remains computationally expensive. Here we present Clinical System One (CS1), a 4-billion-parameter decision model for fast, typed judgments from clinical records, along with two agentic harnesses in which CS1 works together with a generalist language model. CS1-4B is trained on 12.4 million questions and answers from 3.6 million patients across a multi-hospital health system, combining structured-data keys, observed outcomes and language-model supervision across clinical notes, diagnostic reports and patient timelines. It answers multiple typed questions in a single forward pass without task-specific retraining, and each answer carries a probability that can route uncertain cases to human review. On 963,408 held-out patients, CS1-4B outperformed open decision models up to 27 billion parameters on 13 of 14 tasks scored independently of its training teacher. Across 21 external data sets, its aggregate performance approached that of the strongest tested 27-billion-parameter model, with 6.4-fold faster inference in a matched workload. Integrating CS1-4B with a language model agent produced cited answers over complete multi-year patient histories and screened a patient population against the eligibility criteria of 17 registered clinical trials, placing four times as many judged-eligible patients among its top 20 candidates as keyword search while using 690-fold fewer language-model tokens than a language model reading every record. These findings support a division of labour in clinical AI, with small decision models performing repeated record reading and generative models formulating questions and synthesizing evidence.

title: Electronic Health Record Coding of Self-Reported Diagnoses in the All of Us Research Program
desc: Importance: Conditions that are hard to diagnose, several more common in women, may be missing from electronic health records (EHRs), hiding patients from research cohorts and case finding. Objective: To measure how often the EHR contains a diagnosis code for chronic conditions that participants report, and to compare this with national survey benchmarks. Design, Setting, and Participants: This cross-sectional study used the All of Us Research Program Registered Tier Dataset v9. Participants were adults with EHR visits in both 12-month periods from July 2021 to June 2023 who completed a health history survey. We analyzed the data in October 2026. Exposures: Self-reported clinician diagnosis of 10 conditions with ongoing visits or treatment, as well as sex at birth, race and ethnicity, age, and years of EHR records. Main Outcomes and Measures: Share of participants reporting current care who had a qualifying diagnosis code, alone and relative to hypertension and type 2 diabetes, and the ratio of age-standardized coded shares to national survey prevalence. Results: Of 161,480 respondents, 114,610 (73,870 female [64.5%], median [IQR] age 63 [50-72] years) had at least 5 years of EHR records before the survey. Among those reporting current care, 84.6% (95% CI, 84.2%-85.0%) with hypertension and 87.0% (95% CI, 86.5%-87.6%) with type 2 diabetes had a code, compared with 41.3% (95% CI, 38.9%-43.8%) for endometriosis, 39.4% (95% CI, 34.3%-44.8%) for Lyme disease, and 24.4% (95% CI, 23.2%-25.6%) for chronic fatigue. Counting ICD-9-CM and other mapped codes, 55.3%, 51.5%, and 28.3%, respectively, had any qualifying record. Women had lower coded shares than men for hypertension, type 2 diabetes, obesity, depression, and anxiety (crude ratios 0.93-0.96, within-health-system ratios 0.98-1.02) and higher shares for migraine and fibromyalgia (within health systems, 1.11 [95% CI, 1.07-1.15] and 1.41 [95% CI, 1.29-1.57]). Age-standardized coded shares among active patients were 1.1 to 2.4 times national prevalence of the same self-reported diagnoses. Conclusions and Relevance: In this cross-sectional study, fewer than half of participants reporting ongoing care for chronic fatigue, Lyme disease, or endometriosis had a qualifying ICD-10-CM code. Linking each participant's report to their own record measured this gap directly.

title: A Multidimensional Arithmetical Ontology for High-Parameter Cytometry: Gaussian Primes and Cryptographic Hashing for Cell Population Standardization
desc: Background. The rapid expansion of high-dimensional single-cell technologies has outpaced the development of standardized metadata infrastructure. Current text-based nomenclature for cell populations and gating strategies lacks computational rigor, hindering cross-study reproducibility and automated machine learning. Our previous mathematical frameworks, the Prime Population System (PPS) and the Unique Gating Identifier (UGI), proposed arithmetical solutions but were limited by biological fragility (no inherent link between a protein and its structural isoforms) and by computational bottlenecks caused by exponential integer growth. Objective. To develop a scalable, multidimensional arithmetical ontology that unambiguously identifies cell populations and hierarchical gating strategies without biological ambiguity or computational overflow. Methods. We transition the base marker dictionary from the one-dimensional real axis to the complex plane of Gaussian integers (a+bi). The reviewed human proteome of the UniProt Knowledgebase is paired with Gaussian primes satisfying a > b > 0, each list being totally ordered by a key intrinsic to it, so that the pairing is determined by position alone. Each protein receives a contiguous reserved block of 64 primes: slot 0 addresses the protein with isoform unresolved, and slot k addresses UniProt isoform k, the slot index being read directly off the accession. A Bipartite Complex Ontology encodes positive (a+bi) and negative (b+ai) expression states through Conjugate Pair Symmetry. To bypass the 64-bit integer limits of Goedel exponentiation, hierarchical gating sequences are held as vectorized arrays of complex numbers and compressed by SHA-256 deterministic hashing. Results. Pairing against the reference release assigns 53,296 identifiers, 20,431 protein-level and 32,865 isoform-level, with no collisions and no manual curation at any step. Every isoform record in the release resolves under a single rule, including the 329 records whose accession prefix differs from the entry that cites them. The geometric symmetry conserves biological state, distinguishing positive, negative and isoform-resolved expression upon factorization over [Z][i]. title: A generalizable deep learning model for predicting opioid use disorder using language modeling for cross-EHR data harmonization
desc: The opioid use disorder (OUD) epidemic in the United States has been a major public health crisis. We developed OUD-REY ( OUD R isk E valuator at 1 Y ear) - a deep learning model that uses longitudinal electronic health record (EHR) data from the All of Us research program to predict risk of OUD at one year for patients with an opioid prescription. On internal validation, OUD-REY achieved an AUROC of 91.2% and AUPRC of 77.0%. We leveraged a pretrained language model to accommodate thousands of unseen, out-of-vocabulary clinical features in a patient’s longitudinal EHR history. We externally validated our model on a new dataset released by All of Us that was temporally separated from our development set and on a dataset containing ~6 million patients from medical centers of the Veterans Affairs (VA) nationwide over a span of 20 years. On external validation, our model had an AUROC and AUPRC of 86.4% and 23.1% (OUD prevalence of 2.9%), respectively, on our temporally separated All of Us validation set. It had an AUROC and AUPRC of 85.5% and 19.5% (OUD prevalence of 3.5%), respectively, on the VA dataset. Our fairness auditing showed that the model was generally fair for patients with different genders, race, and ethnic backgrounds. This model may potentially improve prevention and care of OUD.

title: The potential of AI inspired approaches for patient monitoring in drug development for Huntington's disease: capturing the digital exhaust for activities of daily living.
desc: [Frontiers in molecular medicine] Diagnosis, assessment and monitoring of Huntington's disease (HD) requires measurement of a complex array of motor, cognitive and psychiatric symptoms over sustained periods. However, the prodromal stages often span over a decade with symptoms presenting in a non-linear manner with short term fluctuations. This presents challenges for investigational drug development as treatment effects may become masked. To help address this issue, a number of digital health technology tools are being investigated for use in HD studies with increasing degrees of utility and sophistication. Herein we outline how remote passive monitoring technologies could be integrated into managed care of HD patients, and have the potential to inform algorithms and digital tools which could be used to improve our understanding of disease trajectories and improve early detection rates. Steps to implementation and the potential to derive learnings from adjacent technologies is presented, affording a key opportunity for next- generation approaches to patient monitoring. Measures derived from such technologies will also provide data to capture disease progression and treatment effects with high fidelity and granularity, and complement existing clinical research outcomes (clinROs) and patient reported outcomes (PRO's). Given the ethical, economic, and societal burden presented by neurodegenerative diseases, such developments could have long term impact in managed healthcare.

title: AI-ECG Detection of Occlusion Myocardial Infarction at Emergency Department Triage (TRIACS)
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: University Medical Centre Maribor; conditions: Acute Coronary Syndromes, Chest Pain, Myocardial Infarction (MI), NSTEMI - Non-ST Segment Elevation MI, ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction; type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 1000; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] Chest pain is among the most common reasons people attend an emergency department, and the electrocardiogram (ECG) recorded at triage is the first test used to decide who needs urgent treatment for a blocked coronary artery. Recognising the ECG patterns that indicate an acutely blocked artery is difficult. Many such patterns do not produce the classic ST-segment elevation, and identifying them reliably requires a level of ECG expertise that is not always available at the point of triage - particularly at night and among clinicians who are not cardiologists. Artificial intelligence (AI) models that read the 12-lead ECG have been shown in several retrospective studies, mainly from Western Europe and the United States, to identify acute coronary occlusion more sensitively than conventional interpretation. These models are now in clinical use in a number of health systems. Their performance has not been assessed in a prospectively enrolled, unselected Slovenian emergency department population, and diagnostic accuracy commonly declines when a model is applied outside the setting in which it was developed. TRIACS is a prospective, single-centre, observational external validation study in the Emergency Department of University Medical Centre Maribor. All consecutive adults presenting with symptoms suggestive of acute coronary syndrome who have a 12-lead ECG recorded at triage as part of routine care will be enrolled. Each triage ECG is analysed by the AI model. The model's output is withheld from all treating clinicians and plays no part in patient care; every patient receives standard guideline-directed management. The main aim is to measure how accurately the AI model identifies angiographically confirmed occlusion myocardial infarction in this population, and to compare its accuracy with the triage decision actually made by the clinical team. The study is therefore designed to inform an adoption decision in either direction, rather than to demonstrate a predetermined conclusion.

title: Fairness or Fallacy? Mapping the Landscape of AI Bias in Disease Detection
desc: Artificial intelligence (AI) has several transformative effects on healthcare, like to facilitate clinicians in disease detection and to manage patient care with enhanced precision. Due to the increasing complexity of medical data and the growing volume of diagnostic images, the substantial computational power needed to process such information creates both opportunities and challenges. To accomplish this objective, numerous methodologies have been proposed to integrate AI into disease detection systems. All these methodologies consider different aspects of clinical diagnosis, considering key parameters such as the type of AI model employed, the nature of input data, and the population demographics being analysed. In this paper, we review different state-of-the-art techniques which have been proposed for various areas of disease detection, specifically focusing on bias identification and mitigation. The proposed solutions are distinguished based on the type of input data they utilize, the architecture of model, and type of bias (algorithmic bias, demographic bias, model bias, and deployment bias). The time frame chosen to filter out relevant studies is between 2015 and 2026. Eventually, we review 23 related articles out of 64,389 analyzed from seven different digital libraries. The obtained results guide us to reach a conclusion with respect to state-of-the-art selected studies. Furthermore, these results reveal significant research gaps that can assist researchers in addressing AI-related bias in medical diagnosis. By prioritizing explainability, data diversity, and fairness in algorithmic design, as well as equitable access for affected patient populations, they can utilize available healthcare resources more effectively.

title: Long COVID undercoding and prediction from releasable electronic health record summaries in All of Us
desc: Objective: To estimate Long COVID undercoding in electronic health records (EHRs) against federal survey prevalence, and to evaluate a predictor of later coding that anyone can rebuild from counts a research enclave releases. Materials and Methods: Among 23,790 All of Us adults with COVID-19, we compared coded shares with Household Pulse Survey prevalence. Among 23,300 adults uncoded at day 90, we predicted a first U09.9 code by day 455. We fitted naive Bayes and linear discriminant models outside the enclave from released counts and compared them with an elastic net fitted inside to the same patients and features. Tests were a random 20% of patients (4,680, 50 coded) and 18 held-out EHR sites (5,760, 60 coded). Results: Under survey-comparability assumptions, about 1 in 9 adults who ever had Long COVID carried its code, and the women-to-men coding ratio was 0.79 (95% sensitivity interval, 0.65-0.95). The released models' areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROCs) were 0.68 (95% CI, 0.60-0.75) on the patient test and 0.64 (0.55-0.72) at held-out sites, 0.049 (0.001-0.104) above the elastic net. On the patient test, the elastic net had a higher area under the precision-recall curve (difference 0.062, 0.003-0.122). Released probabilities overestimated coding risk at held-out sites. Discussion: Fitting from released counts did not consistently lower discrimination. Coded outcomes inform disease discrimination only under stated coding assumptions. Conclusion: Long COVID is substantially and unevenly undercoded, and a model rebuilt from public counts predicts its later coding with moderate discrimination.

title: BiHC: Protein domain segmentation by bidirectional hierarchical clustering using Voronoi tessellation and physical self-containment
desc: Protein domains are commonly regarded as structurally separated, functionally relevant, and evolutionarily separable units. Although classification systems may assign different domain boundaries to the same structure, structural separation remains a shared criterion, and many domain parsers assess it through inter-residue distances, contact numbers, or contact densities. However, the Voronoi contact area, which is widely used to study protein-protein interactions and predict contact sites, has seen limited use in domain parsing. There are two potential challenges to this problem. First, unlike in protein-protein interaction, partitions are not known in advance and must be identified before their interface can be evaluated. Second, the contact area depends on fragment size and internal packing, making it difficult to compare candidate partitions. Here, we introduce BiHC (Bidirectional Hierarchical Clustering), a domain parser based on all-heavy-atom Voronoi contact areas. By normalizing the contact area for fragment size and internal packing, and incorporating residue hydropathy, we define a pairwise self-containment score F. BiHC applies F in two independent hierarchical searches: top-down recursive splitting until no admissible division remains, and bottom-up merging of secondary-structure elements until the entire structure becomes a single fragment. Intermediate partitions from both searches are ranked by a global partition quality score G, derived on the same principle. On two CATH-ECOD consensus benchmarks, under balanced evaluation, BiHC achieved the strongest performance among all tested criterion-based parsers and was comparable to Chainsaw, the best-performing deep learning method tested. These results show that the Voronoi-based criterion can yield competitive domain parsing.

title: GUARD-LGG: a glioma upfront AI-driven radiotherapy response decipher for lower-grade glioma
desc: Radiotherapy (RT) remains a cornerstone in managing lower-grade glioma (LGG), but its response varies widely. Reliable pre-treatment prediction of RT response could facilitate patient management but remains unavailable. Here we present GUARD-LGG, a machine learning model designed to predict early RT response in LGG before treatment. GUARD-LGG was trained on 963 patients from a major center, tested on 187 patients from seven independent institutions, and 328 patients prospectively enrolled in a registered clinical trial. GUARD-LGG achieved AUCs of 0.946 (95% CI: 0.938–0.962), 0.929 (95% CI: 0.894–0.965), 0.882 (95% CI: 0.830–0.934), and 0.913 (95% CI: 0.878–0.949) in the training, internal validation, external, and prospective test sets, respectively. Model interpretation highlighted residual tumor, age, T2-weighted texture roughness and T1-weighted contrast intensity changes as major predictors. Radiogenomic analyses suggested potential associations between predicted unfavorable RT response and enrichment of RT resistance-related pathways. Consistently, patients with predicted unfavorable RT response exhibited shorter overall survival. In conclusion, GUARD-LGG enables individualized prediction of early RT response before therapy, offering a tool for pre-treatment response stratification in LGG.

title: Reinforcement Learning in Healthcare Analytics: Transforming Personalised Medicine and Clinical Decision-Making.
source: PubMed · Journal of evaluation in clinical practice
desc: [Journal of evaluation in clinical practice] Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as a promising artificial intelligence paradigm for adaptive and sequential decision-making in healthcare, enabling personalised treatment optimisation and intelligent clinical resource management beyond the capabilities of conventional static models. This review aims to examine recent advances in RL for healthcare analytics, focusing on its applications, emerging techniques, challenges, and future research directions. The review studies model-free, model-based, deep reinforcement learning, and multi-agent reinforcement learning techniques applied to personalised treatment planning, chronic disease management, clinical decision support, healthcare resource optimisation, and robotic-assisted healthcare. It also explores Federated Reinforcement Learning (FRL), Explainable Reinforcement Learning (XRL), and longitudinal outcome prediction. The reviewed studies utilise healthcare datasets, including the Osteoporosis Dataset, UCI Heart Disease Dataset, Pima Indians Diabetes Dataset, SEER Cancer Dataset, and MIMIC-IV Dataset. The reviewed studies demonstrate that RL-based approaches support adaptive clinical decision-making, personalised treatment recommendations, improved operational efficiency, and patient outcome prediction. FRL offers opportunities for privacy-preserving collaborative learning, while XRL enhances the transparency and interpretability of clinical decisions. However, challenges remain concerning data quality, reward function design, model interpretability, computational scalability, ethical considerations, and regulatory compliance. R.L has significant potential to advance intelligent healthcare analytics through personalised, adaptive, and efficient clinical solutions. Future research should prioritise privacy preservation, interpretability, scalability, ethical AI, and regulatory compliance to develop safe, reliable, and trustworthy RL-based healthcare systems.

title: Diagnostic Performance of an AI-Based Multi-Omics Model for Early Lung Cancer
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Beijing Chao Yang Hospital; conditions: Pulmonary Nodules, Early Detection of Cancer, Lung Neoplasms; type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 1050; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] This is a prospective, multicenter observational cohort study for patients with lung nodules suspicious for early-stage lung cancer. The study aims to build AI-assisted diagnostic models by integrating clinical data, CT imaging and multi-omics biomarkers, and validate a rapid evaluation system for bronchoscopic biopsy specimens. No investigational drugs or devices will be applied; all participants receive routine clinical care. We will collect clinical records, CT images, blood and tissue samples, and conduct long-term follow-up of disease outcomes. A total of 1050 subjects will be enrolled from 8 participating hospitals in China.

title: From Clinical Risk Prediction to Operational Decisions: An Uncertainty-Aware Framework for ICU Staffing
desc: Advances in electronic health records (EHR) and large-scale critical care databases have enabled the development of machine learning models for the early detection of patient deterioration. While these models often achieve strong predictive performance for outcomes such as sepsis and mortality, most studies evaluate them purely on discrimination metrics. This leaves a critical gap: how to systematically translate probabilistic clinical risk estimates into downstream operational decisions under real-world constraints, such as shift rigidity and hiring delays. This study proposes an uncertainty-aware anticipatory staffing framework that bridges short-term patient risk prediction and staff planning without altering the upstream predictive model. Instead of relying on naive deterministic aggregation or fixed safety buffers, the framework explicitly models dynamic predictive uncertainty and evaluates extreme shortage exposure using Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR). These aggregated, risk-calibrated demand signals are then embedded into an hourly rolling-horizon scheduling policy to generate delay-constrained staffing decisions. Evaluated on realistic trajectories from the MIMIC-IV database, the proposed framework demonstrates a favorable cost-shortage trade-off compared to deterministic and purely reactive baselines. Pareto frontier analysis illustrates how uncertainty-aware demand construction changes resource allocation under varying safety preferences, while stress testing confirms the framework's operational robustness even when subjected to systematic predictive bias in the form of calibration drift. By formalizing this translation layer, this work provides a principled, transparent pathway for safely integrating probabilistic AI outputs into high-stakes healthcare operational systems.

title: Self-reported diagnoses as training labels for finding uncoded chronic fatigue, fibromyalgia, and endometriosis in the All of Us Research Program
desc: Objective: Case-finding models for underdiagnosed conditions are usually trained on diagnosis codes, which are missing from the records of many patients with a clinical diagnosis. We asked whether models trained on self-reported diagnoses rank uncoded self-reporters higher than models trained on later codes, and how a score fit only from released summary counts compares with a participant-level model. Methods: In the All of Us Research Program, we followed survey respondents with no qualifying diagnosis code by the survey date for later codes. For chronic fatigue, fibromyalgia, and endometriosis (participants recorded as female at birth), we fit a naive Bayes score with empirical-Bayes shrinkage, from released feature-by-label counts for the self-reported diagnosis and from exact counts inside the data enclave for a later code, and an elastic net on participant-level data for each label. In a random 20% validation split, we measured discrimination of self-report, of uncoded self-reporters (no qualifying code observed), and of later codes. Results: For chronic fatigue (149,860 respondents, including 7,770 self-reporters, 95% with no code observed), the summary-count score trained on self-report ranked uncoded self-reporters with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.74 (95% CI, 0.72-0.75), against 0.67 (95% CI, 0.65-0.69) when trained on later codes. For later codes, the two scores were similar (0.69 vs 0.70). Fibromyalgia showed the same pattern (0.73 vs 0.64 and 0.74 vs 0.72). Elastic nets trained on self-report ranked uncoded self-reporters higher than the summary-count scores (0.80 vs 0.74 and 0.78 vs 0.73) but discriminated later codes less well than code-trained elastic nets. For endometriosis, the self-report score also ranked uncoded self-reporters above the code-trained score (0.61 vs 0.53), but discrimination was low and it did not discriminate later codes (0.50 vs 0.70). Conclusion: The choice of training label changes which patients a case-finding model ranks highly. For all 3 conditions, self-reported diagnoses were the more useful label for finding uncoded self-reporters. For chronic fatigue and fibromyalgia, the self-report score also discriminated later codes as well as the code-trained score. Independent clinical validation is needed before these models guide case finding.

title: MEDA-PKD: a dynamic, real-time analytics platform for precision care in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
desc: The use of medical real-world data is constrained by fragmented data infrastructures and the absence of tools integrating longitudinal clinical with molecular data at scale. Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), the most common monogenic cause of kidney failure, exemplifies this gap given its phenotypic complexity and the need for individualized treatment decisions. We present MEDA-PKD (MEdical DAta translation service of Polycystic Kidney Disease), an interactive, near-real-time analytics platform that integrates clinical routine with research data from the German AD(H)PKD Tolvaptan Registry (NCT02497521, DRKS00008910) into a harmonized database ( https://doi.org/10.18716/adpkd_registry ). MEDA-PKD provides automated near-real-time analysis and dynamic visualization, replacing traditional static approaches to clinical cohorts. As of March 2026, MEDA-PKD visualized data from 1735 patients (mean follow-up 796 days). eGFR slope analysis of data from patients initiating tolvaptan therapy (332 patients) demonstrates the platform’s capacity to evaluate real-world therapeutic impact in real-time. Other tabs include family history, medication, lifestyle, quality of life and a wide array of lab values (20,894 entries). Besides, MEDA-PKD integrates proteomics data and allows for secure individual patient-level data access. MEDA-PKD represents a paradigm shift by transforming static cohort data into a living, actionable knowledge resource in ADPKD and will serve as a template for other diseases.

title: Design of Screening Cardiometabolic Opportunities Using Transformative Echocardiography Artificial Intelligence (SCOUT-Echo-AI).
desc: [American heart journal] Steatotic liver disease (SLD) is highly prevalent among individuals with cardiovascular disease, but often remains undiagnosed until advanced sequelae such as fibrotic liver disease and hepatocellular carcinoma develop. ​​Transthoracic echocardiography routinely captures incidental subcostal views of the liver that are not used clinically. The EchoNet-Liver algorithm uses artificial intelligence (AI) to predict the presence of liver disease based on routine clinical echocardiograms. Prospective evaluation in real-world practice is needed to understand the clinical utility and impact of AI-enabled opportunistic liver disease screening. The SCOUT-Echo-AI study is a single-arm, prospective, multicenter, open-label pragmatic interventional trial that will be conducted across six diverse U.S. healthcare systems (Kaiser Permanente Northern California, Stanford Healthcare, Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, University of California Los Angeles, Northwestern Medicine, and Massachusetts General Brigham). Routine echocardiograms will be analyzed by the EchoNet-Liver AI algorithm with an estimated enrollment of ∼3,000 patients. Treating clinicians or participants themselves will be notified of potential undiagnosed liver disease with site-specific workflows in place to ensure routine clinical care for definitive case confirmation. Primary outcomes will be SLD and fibrotic liver disease detection rates and positive predictive values within 12 months of AI identification. Pre-specified secondary outcomes will assess diagnostic accuracy against other gold-standard modalities, treatment initiation, time to diagnosis, and impact on other clinical events. Outcomes will be compared against historical usual-care and contemporary below-threshold cohorts. SCOUT-Echo-AI is a prospective multicenter study evaluating the real-world impact of AI-enabled opportunistic liver disease screening using routine echocardiography.

title: AI-CARE: A Novel AI-Driven Mobile Insulin Calculator Integrating Image- Based Carbohydrate Estimation and CGM
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Tan Tock Seng Hospital; conditions: Diabetes Mellitus; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 48; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] AI-CARE is an artificial intelligence-enabled clinical decision support mobile application designed to support prandial insulin dosing in individuals receiving MDI, incorporating a "human-in-the-loop" approach to ensure user verification of recommended doses. The application integrates AI-driven image-based carbohydrate estimation tailored to Asian dietary contexts, individualized patient-specific insulin parameters, and real-time CGM data to generate personalized insulin dose recommendations. The primary objective of this study is to evaluate the feasibility, safety, and preliminary effectiveness of the AI-CARE mobile application among adults with diabetes receiving MDI. Feasibility will be assessed in terms of recruitment, retention, participant adherence, and application usability. Safety will be evaluated by monitoring the incidence of hypoglycaemia, hyperglycaemia, and other adverse events throughout the intervention period. The study will also examine the preliminary effectiveness of AI-CARE on glycaemic and patient-reported outcomes compared with usual care. In addition, a qualitative process evaluation will be conducted to explore participants' experiences and perceptions of using AI-CARE, including perceived ease of use, usefulness, acceptability, and barriers and facilitators to real-world implementation. Findings from this phase will inform further refinement and optimization of the AI-CARE system and guide the design of a future large- scale randomized controlled trial.

title: CODA: Cohort- and Drift-aware Foundation Model for Multimodal Clinical Reasoning
desc: Recent advances in multimodal foundation models have demonstrated strong performance across diverse clinical tasks. However, existing approaches predominantly operate at the individual sample level and fail to model the interplay between population-level cohort patterns and patient-specific variation that underlie real-world clinical reasoning. In practice, clinicians routinely reason through patient cohorts sharing similar demographic, physiological, or pathological characteristics, while accounting for patient-specific deviations from the group prototype. Motivated by this gap, we propose CODA, a cohort- and drift-aware foundation model for multimodal clinical reasoning. CODA explicitly integrates cohort structure into the modeling pipeline through two complementary mechanisms: cohort-aware population stratification and drift-aware individual adaptation. In particular, we leverage reinforcement learning to discover clinically meaningful patient cohorts, and further model each patient's deviation from cohort prototypes as a structured drift signal encoding fine-grained individual heterogeneity. These cohort- and drift-aware representations are incorporated into the foundation model to enable reasoning that is simultaneously informed by population-level patterns and sensitive to individual-level variation. Extensive experiments on real-world electronic health record (EHR) benchmarks demonstrate that CODA achieves consistent effectiveness and strong generalizability across diverse clinical tasks, including closed-QA, open-QA, and report generation.

title: Interpretable Phenotype Discovery Using Temporal Risk-Aware Clustering
desc: Longitudinal clinical cohorts contain heterogeneous progression patterns that are obscured by coarse diagnostic labels. Discovering these latent progression phenotypes requires models that distinguish patients not only by their outcomes, but also by how their clinical trajectories evolve. This paper proposes TRACE, an interpretable temporal phenotyping method that enables the learning of outcome-informed progression phenotypes from longitudinal trajectories. TRACE combines a trajectory- and outcome-aware contrastive objective with a probabilistic predictive phenotype layer, encouraging phenotypes to capture progression structure while remaining predictive of diagnostic state. A dual-attention mechanism further supports interpretation by identifying the visits and clinical variables most associated with each phenotype assignment. TRACE is evaluated on the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) cohort for cognitive disease modeling, showing improved performance in both diagnostic prediction and phenotype discovery compared with other temporal phenotyping baselines. Finally, by allowing the number of phenotypes to exceed the diagnostic labels, TRACE enables discovering additional progression patterns that are not captured by labels defined a priori.

title: Extending synthetic medical education: generating OSCE cases with LLMs
desc: Objective Structured Clinical Examinations (OSCEs) are central to competency-based medical education, yet high-quality case development is resource-intensive. Large language models (LLMs) offer a scalable solution, but comprehensive OSCE case generation, including components such as candidate instructions, standardized patient scripts, and examiner marking schemes, is underexplored. We developed an LLM-based tool to generate complete OSCE stations. Three board-certified internists evaluated 24 generated cases across eight internal medicine diagnoses and three learner levels using a 12-item Likert instrument. Ratings were high across all domains; communication behaviors (4.64/5), EPA alignment (4.62/5), and overall value (4.61/5) performed best; guideline concordance scored lowest (4.24/5) with the greatest rater disagreement. As a feasibility study, these findings establish that whole, schema-validated OSCE stations can be generated from a single structured call at a quality experts rate as acceptable, while also identifying guideline concordance and difficult calibration as the domains most requiring faculty oversight -- providing reproducible infrastructure for, but not yet evidence of, effective EPA-aligned OSCE development.

title: Single-cell RNA sequencing combined with artificial intelligence to uncover immunotherapy biomarkers and decipher drug resistance mechanisms in glioblastoma.
desc: [Frontiers in oncology] Glioblastoma represents the most aggressive primary malignant tumor of the central nervous system, characterized by extensive intratumoral heterogeneity, profound immunosuppression, therapeutic resistance, and poor clinical outcomes. Although immunotherapy has revolutionized cancer treatment, its clinical efficacy in GBM remains limited, largely due to the complexity of the tumor ecosystem and the lack of validated predictive biomarkers. Recent advances in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), spatial transcriptomics, and artificial intelligence (AI)-based computational approaches have provided unprecedented opportunities to decipher tumor heterogeneity and identify clinically actionable biomarkers. This mini-review integrates studies related to scRNA-seq and its combination technology, further elaborating on the tumor plasticity, immune suppression, and metabolic-epigenetic reprogramming mechanisms of GBM. The article systematically summarizes the complete analysis process of integrating single-cell multi-omics data by AI and highlights the application value of AI in validating biomarkers. The above research ideas are expected to overcome clinical resistance problems, optimize patient stratification schemes, and enhance the efficacy of immunotherapy, providing theoretical support for developing highly stable prognostic biomarkers and achieving individualized precise immunotherapy for glioblastoma.

title: Comparing AI and Standard Pregnancy Chatbots
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Nivi, Inc.; conditions: Pregnancy, Prenatal Care, Maternal Health; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 2500; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] Many pregnant women in India use mobile phones to get health information. Nivi runs a free WhatsApp service called askNivi that answers questions about pregnancy and sends reminders about prenatal care visits. The current version of askNivi replies using a set of prepared answers. This study tests a new version that uses artificial intelligence to write replies. The new version looks up information in a reviewed collection of maternal health materials before answering, so its replies stay grounded in checked sources. It is also designed to recognize symptoms that may signal a pregnancy complication and to tell the user to seek care right away. Women who join the study are assigned at random to one of the two versions. Neither version replaces medical care, and both send the same weekly messages and clinic reminders. Women can ask questions at any time throughout their pregnancy. The study will look at how much women use each version, how useful they find it, how they decide when to seek care, and whether they attend prenatal care visits. About 2,500 pregnant women in Assam, Madhya Pradesh, and Uttar Pradesh will take part. Participation lasts from enrollment, between 10 and 20 weeks of pregnancy, until delivery.

title: TRACE: Tracking Multimodal Clinical Trajectories for Inpatient Risk Prediction
desc: Accurate inpatient risk prediction requires modeling heterogeneous clinical evidence that accumulates irregularly over time. This challenge spans in-hospital mortality, prolonged length of stay, and readmission, each with task-specific observation windows. Existing multimodal approaches combine structured health record data, chest x-rays, and clinical text, but primarily focus on modality fusion or missing-modality compensation, with limited attention to temporal trajectories over an admission. We propose TRACE (TRAjectory modeling of multimodal Clinical Events), a daily-scale framework organizing clinical events into day-level trajectories, separating day-invariant global context from day-specific local events drawn from EHR data, chest x-rays, radiology reports, and discharge summaries. The trajectory is encoded using temporal attention, allowing unavailable modalities to emit no tokens. A phenotype-guided contrastive objective further organizes admissions under heterogeneous disease distributions. Across cohorts from MIMIC-IV, eICU, and MIMIC-III comprising nearly 180,000 total stays, we evaluate TRACE on mortality, length of stay, and readmission prediction. TRACE achieves the highest AUROC across all nine dataset-task settings and the highest ACC in eight, outperforming baselines. Ablation studies validate our attention masks and contrastive learning, while trajectory-level attribution localizes risk-associated hospital days and modalities.

title: Physiologic digital twins for decision support in multi-day ex vivo organ perfusion
desc: Many potentially recoverable donor livers are discarded because current paradigms prioritize preservation and viability assessment over prolonged stabilization and rehabilitation. Multi-day normothermic ex vivo perfusion creates a therapeutic window but shifts the challenge from sustaining circulation to interpreting evolving physiologic trajectories without native homeostatic regulation. We propose physiologic digital twins that integrate mechanistic and statistical models to estimate organ state and support decision-making during ex vivo perfusion.

title: The Ambulatory Patient Experience with Ambient Artificial Intelligence Scribes: A Qualitative Study.
source: PubMed · Journal of general internal medicine
desc: [Journal of general internal medicine] The effect of ambient artificial intelligence (AI) scribes on patient experience remains understudied and has been largely limited to closed-ended surveys. Qualitative studies are needed to more fully explore how ambient AI scribes influence patient experience. The aim of this study was to explore how ambient AI scribes influence the patient experience and to identify factors that improve patients' comfort with these tools. We conducted a qualitative study using a semi-structured interview guide that captured key patient experience domains from a literature review. We recruited patients from numerous ambulatory specialties (e.g., dermatology, primary care) whose clinicians were participating in a pragmatic randomized clinical trial of an ambient AI scribe implementation at an academic medical center. We deductively and inductively drew patterns in patients' reported experiences and the factors that contributed to patients' comfort with these tools. Twenty patients were included in our sample before thematic saturation occurred. Patients reported improvements in patient experience through increased respect for patients' preferences (e.g., fewer distractions), improved thoroughness of visit notes, and increased time spent answering patients' questions. Factors influencing comfort included demographic factors (e.g., exposure to similar technologies), lack of saliency of the device, lack of privacy-related concerns, positive pre-existing patient-clinician relationships, and anticipated benefits to care. Ambient AI scribes may improve the patient experience through improved patient-clinician verbal, non-verbal, and written communication. These findings contribute to our understanding how these tools shape the patient experience. Not applicable.

title: Remote Digital Assessments for Cognitive Disorders
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Centre for Addiction and Mental Health; conditions: Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI), Alzheimer Disease (AD); type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 60; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] Memory and thinking problems in older adults, including mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and Alzheimer's disease (AD), can be difficult to assess promptly because evaluation often depends on in-person specialist visits. MonitorCog-AI is a computer-based platform designed to provide a more accessible way to assess and monitor cognitive changes using standard computers or tablets. Artificial intelligence (AI) will be used to analyze the digital information collected by the platform and examine whether combining several types of measures improves assessment of cognitive impairment. The study will include 60 adults aged 50 years and older: 20 healthy adults, 20 adults with MCI, and 20 adults with AD. Participants will be assessed at baseline, 6 months, and 12 months. At each timepoint, participants will complete one clinical assessment and one digital assessment. The clinical assessment will include standard measures of memory and thinking, an assessment of daily functioning, and a brief recording of brain electrical activity. The digital assessment will take approximately 60-80 minutes and will assess five areas: cognition, eye movements measured using a webcam, language, speech, and fine-motor performance measured using a mouse. At baseline, the digital assessment will be completed in the clinic; at 6 and 12 months, it will usually be completed remotely at home. The study has three main goals. First, it will determine whether MonitorCog-AI is feasible, acceptable, easy to use, and not overly burdensome for repeated assessment. Second, it will examine how well AI-based analysis of the digital measures distinguishes healthy adults, adults with MCI, and adults with AD, and whether combining several types of digital information performs better than any single type alone. Third, it will examine how digital measures change over 12 months and whether these changes are related to changes in clinical measures of cognition and daily functioning.

title: Localization Gains from Explanation Regularization Should Not Be Interpreted as Faithfulness Gains.
desc: Training-time explanation regularization is often evaluated by whether saliency maps become more concentrated within annotated regions. We argue that this criterion alone is insufficient: transformation consistency, lesion localization, and faithfulness to the classifier are distinct properties and should be evaluated separately, particularly in medical imaging. We examine this distinction through a case study of Contrastive Grad-CAM Consistency (CGC) in three-class brain tumor MRI classification. Using a single-channel ResNet-50 with five-fold patient-grouped cross-validation, we compare a cross-entropy baseline with CGC. CGC changes overall Pointing Game (PG) from $27.24\%$ to $36.02\%$ and Relevance Mass Accuracy (RMA) from $11.17\%$ to $18.01\%$, while classification accuracy changes from $93.63\%$ to $94.87\%$. Perturbation-based faithfulness metrics show inconsistent changes: Insertion Area Under the Curve (IAUC) changes from $0.73$ to $0.78$, whereas Deletion Area Under the Curve (DAUC) favors the baseline ($0.36$ versus $0.41$; lower is better), and overall Iterative Removal Of Features (IROF) is $0.57$ for both models. These results support our position that improved spatial agreement with pathology should not be interpreted as a general improvement in explanation faithfulness. We therefore recommend property-specific evaluation in which the property targeted by the explanation objective, spatial agreement with reference regions, and model reliance are measured and reported separately.

Reinforcement learning for repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation protocol selection in treatment-resistant depression
desc: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), including intermittent theta-burst stimulation (iTBS), is an established treatment for treatment-resistant depression, but clinicians lack evidence-based guidance for session-level choices among stimulation type, intensity, and laterality. In this study, we investigated whether a reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm trained on routine clinical data could recommend session-level rTMS protocols associated with greater symptom improvement using electronic health record data from 1609 adults treated with rTMS between January 2023 and June 2025 across 19 clinic groups. Among 370 patients from held-out clinics, treatment decisions matching algorithm recommendations were associated with 0.788 points greater next-session Patient Health Questionnaire-9 improvement than treatments that differed (95% CI: 0.634–0.940). Following every recommendation was projected to produce 3.22 points of additional improvement (95% CI: 2.72–3.75). These findings suggest RL can find treatment patterns associated with greater next-session improvement and potentially meaningful improvement accumulated across a treatment episode.

title: Point-of-care Ultrasound: Past, Present, and Future.
desc: [Journal of medical ultrasound] Point-of-care ultrasound (PoCUS) has fundamentally transformed clinical practice from comprehensive, organ-based imaging into a rapid, goal-directed bedside tool. The development of standardized protocols - such as focused assessment with sonography for trauma, rapid ultrasound for shock and hypotension, and bedside lung ultrasound in emergency - along with real-time procedural guidance, has established PoCUS as an essential competency in critical care and emergency medicine. Currently, technological advancements have miniaturized ultrasound devices, dismantling geographical barriers and facilitating decentralized healthcare models. In the emergency department (ED), the early integration of PoCUS significantly reduces the ED length of stay and optimizes resource utilization, whereas its application continues to expand into general inpatient and community care. Looking forward, the democratization of medical education and the convergence of wireless technology with artificial intelligence will further minimize operator dependence. As its diagnostic value is firmly established, future research must pivot toward quantifying patient-centered outcomes, such as mortality and hospital readmission rates, solidifying PoCUS as an indispensable pillar of modern medicine.

title: XGLASS: X-Ray, Gaze and Language Assisted Slice Sequencing for CT Volumes
desc: Vision-language models (VLMs) achieve remarkable performance on 2D medical images, such as X-rays or pathology images, while 3D VLMs that directly process CT/MRI volumes lag behind due to limited 3D training data and the predominance of 2D foundation architectures. To leverage powerful 2D VLMs for analyzing medical volumes, which contain hundreds of slices, it is therefore necessary to focus only on those few slices, which are diagnostically relevant. To enable such a prioritization, we propose XGLASS, a method that transfers medical expertise from 2D X-rays to 3D CT for task-aware slice prioritization. XGLASS uses disease-conditioned importance maps derived from language-aligned radiologist gaze on X-rays and spatially aligns them with coronal CT projections, bringing gaze priors and CT content into a shared 2D representation. The fused gaze-prior/CT projection is then used to predict a disease-specific ordering of axial slices, prioritizing diagnostically relevant slices. XGLASS significantly improves budgeted retrieval over 2D and 3D-native baselines, achieving a top-10 hit rate up to 75.9% for the best-performing disease. In practice, this means that after inspecting only the top 10 slices (4.17% of a 240-slice scan), XGLASS identifies a diagnostically relevant slice in more than 75% of cases. For downstream slice-wise finding classification, an XGLASS-selected 30-slice candidate set reduces model calls by 87.5% while improving F1 by 11.3 percentage points over all-slice inference, 4.2 points over the strongest 2D selector, and remains competitive with 3D-native selectors while requiring up to 130.8 times less time and 10.9 times less GPU memory per finding, supporting its use as a lightweight preselector for volumetric CT analysis. The code and pretrained checkpoint are available on https://github.com/michaelgloeckler/XGLASS.

Endoscopic eradication therapy of Barrett's dysplasia and early adenocarcinoma: where we stand and what's next.
source: PubMed · Diseases of the esophagus : official journal of the International Society for Diseases of the Esophagus
desc: [Diseases of the esophagus : official journal of the International Society for Diseases of the Esophagus] Barrett's esophagus (BE) is the only recognized precursor to esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC). Endoscopic monitoring of BE allows for early detection and prevention against advanced cancer, which carries high morbidity and mortality. Over the past two decades, management of early EAC has shifted from esophagectomy toward organ-preserving endoscopic eradication therapy (EET), including endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR), endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD), and ablative modalities such as radiofrequency ablation, cryotherapy, and hybrid argon plasma coagulation. EMR remains standard for most lesions with pre-invasive neoplasia and small intramucosal EAC, while ESD provides technical advantages for larger or complex neoplasia, though comparative long-term outcome data are limited. Ablation after resection achieves durable clearance of dysplasia and intestinal metaplasia, with emerging therapies showing promise in refractory or high-risk cases. Structured post-EET surveillance is critical, as recurrence risk is highest within 1-2 years of achieving remission, but persists at lower levels long-term. The risk of recurrence is influenced by lesion characteristics, treatment strategy, and center experience. Personalized, risk-adapted surveillance is increasingly supported, incorporating clinical factors such as BE length, baseline histology and prior treatment. More recently, molecular biomarkers and artificial intelligence (AI)-driven integration of clinical and genomic features have shown promising results. Future research should optimize tissue acquisition, refine biomarker panels, and validate AI-enabled predictive models to improve patient selection, minimize recurrence, and guide cost-effective, individualized care.

title: REST: Reliability-Guided Spatial Transcriptomics Supervision for Gene Expression Prediction from Histopathological HE-Stained Images
desc: Histopathology is central to cancer diagnosis, but morphology in Hematoxylin and Eosin (HE)-stained images does not directly reveal the molecular states that characterize disease heterogeneity and inform tumor characterization, prognostic assessment, and biomarker discovery. Spatial Transcriptomics (ST) measures spatially resolved gene expression, providing molecular information within tissue architecture, yet differences in assay coverage and spot informativeness make paired HE--ST observations unequally reliable for representation learning. We propose Reliability-Guided Spatial Transcriptomics (REST) supervision with Biological Program Bank (BPB), a program-structured and reliability-guided ST-supervised training framework for predicting molecular information from H\&E images. REST constructs BPB from curated signature, pathway, and cell-type gene sets to provide a shared structure for ST encoding, reliability estimation, and molecular reconstruction. Guided by BPB, Spot-Reliability Contrastive Alignment (SRCA) measures the reliability of each spot from assay-level program coverage and spot-level activity dispersion, and reweights HE--ST alignment accordingly. Biology-Informed Program Reconstruction (BIPR) further uses learnable program queries to reconstruct member-gene expression from histological morphology. REST's training corpus comprised 209 samples (407,475 spots across 16 organs); evaluation used 70 disjoint samples (230,056 spots across eight organs) for gene-expression, pathway-activity, and cell-signature prediction. REST achieved the highest Macro correlation among state-of-the-art ST-supervised training methods and outperformed existing pathology foundation models. Code is available at https://github.com/lanfz2000/REST.

A hybrid deep learning-based OCR model for handwritten medical prescriptions.
desc: [Frontiers in medicine] The current trend involving the use of paper-based medical prescriptions and the exchange of such by the social media is a major problem in automated and accurate text extraction in healthcare processes. This paper suggests a complete smart pipeline to digitize the images of medical prescriptions with lightweight deep learning-based classification, specialized Optical Character Recognition (OCR) engines, and comparative benchmarking of results using a large language model (LLM). The web scraped images of medical prescriptions are initially processed through a GhostNetV2 classifier to differentiate between handwritten and digital medical prescriptions. According to this choice, digital images are sent to PaddleOCR, and handwritten images are considered in Tesseract OCR so that each image could be processed by the best suitable recognition engine. The OCR outputs from both branches are benchmarked against GPT-4o (OpenAI) as an independent baseline to assess competitive performance and provide error-rate context. Experimental analysis shows that the suggested adaptive routing strategy is characterized by the fact that it has a high classification rate and the character and word error rates are significantly lower than those single-OCR techniques. The system is competitive with, though does not exceed, the raw accuracy of a state-of-the-art LLM-based OCR baseline (GPT-4o), while offering practical advantages in cost, transparency, and on-premises deployability that the black-box, per-call LLM baseline does not. The findings verify that the combination of lightweight classifiers and multi-OCR decision routing and multi-LLM-aided comparative benchmarking offers a scalable and robust solution to real-world medical prescriptions digitization, which adds to better automation, accuracy, and safety in healthcare information processing.

title: Temporal Evidence Allocation For Longitudinal Clinical Retrieval: A Position And Technical Report
desc: Electronic health records are written to support care, not retrieval. Across years of oncology notes, the primary diagnosis is restated in report after report, while the events that shape a patient's course, such as a recurrence or a change in therapy, may be recorded only once. A retriever that ranks passages by similarity to the query keeps returning the repeated material and can miss these transitions, that is, it exhibits temporal redundancy across historical narratives. We argue that longitudinal clinical retrieval should be treated as allocating a limited evidence budget across time, not just ranking by relevance. We separate the task into three objectives: temporal evidence allocation, candidate reconstruction, and clinical validation. In Study A (13 clinical queries over 20 patient records, with two-stage reconstruction), the Temporal-15 configuration reaches a milestone slot recall of 0.538, compared with 0.388 for the Global-50 baseline. However, it also retrieves far more evidence (496 versus 50 indexed units per query), so the gain cannot be credited to allocation alone. When evidence is held fixed, removing prompted precedence rules raises schema-order reversals from 0.010 to 0.080. A five-patient, single-query pilot with fixed budgets finds that wider temporal coverage does not reliably yield more dated milestones. Together, these results suggest that how much a record says about a period is a poor guide to how useful that period is as evidence. Because no expert reference timelines are available, our measurements describe retrieval behavior rather than clinical accuracy. This position and technical report presents the retrieval analysis behind the Onco-CONSTRUE framework and sets out a research agenda for budget-constrained longitudinal clinical retrieval.

The β-cells in type 1 diabetes mellitus: findings from human pancreas studies.
desc: [Nature reviews. Endocrinology] Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by long-term and dynamic interactions between the immune system and pancreatic β-cells, ultimately leading to severe insulin deficiency. A paradigm shift in T1DM research has occurred in the past few years, with research now focusing on the human disease because of access to human pancreatic tissue and pancreas-draining lymph nodes. Advances in high-resolution imaging, single-cell and spatial multi-omics, and histopathology based on artificial intelligence have profoundly reshaped our understanding of disease initiation and progression. These studies revealed that β-cell loss and/or dysfunction might begin earlier than previously appreciated, preferentially affecting small β-cell-rich islets and insulin-positive cell clusters, with larger islets showing transient resistance. Substantial β-cell mass often persists at diagnosis, accompanied by functional impairment rather than immediate cell death. Across disease stages, β-cells exhibit conserved molecular signatures dominated by interferon signalling, enhanced antigen presentation and adaptive immune-evasion programmes, with evidence of heterogeneity linked to age, disease duration and immune context. Parallel analyses of pancreatic lymph nodes show early immune dysregulation, including altered regulatory T cell signatures and expansion of stem-like cytotoxic T cell populations, even before overt hyperglycaemia. Together, these findings support an integrated model of T1DM progression that enables alignment of clinical staging with evolving β-cell and immune phenotypes.

title: HGASurv: Hierarchical Granularity-Aware Integration for Multimodal Survival Prediction
desc: Objective: Multimodal survival prediction jointly analyzes histopathological whole-slide images (WSIs), genomic profiles, and clinical variables to stratify patients by risk. However, existing approaches often inadequately account for granularity differences across modalities, particularly in spatial organization and feature dimensionality. To address these challenges, we propose HGASurv, which introduces a hierarchical WSI encoding module and a clinical-guided graph propagation module for granularity-aware multimodal integration. Methods: The hierarchical WSI encoding module maps WSI patch features onto a spatial grid using their original coordinates and applies parallel convolutions to construct representations at patch, local-neighborhood, and regional scales. Genomic signature embeddings then query these scale-specific WSI representations through cross-modal co-attention, producing signature-conditioned morphological features. The clinical-guided graph propagation module uses clinical variables to define patient-similarity edges and propagates fused image-genomic node embeddings with graph attention, integrating clinical information through topology rather than feature concatenation. Results: Across three TCGA cohorts, HGASurv achieved the strongest overall C-index performance, with ablation studies supporting the complementary contributions of the hierarchical WSI encoding and clinical-guided graph propagation modules. Conclusion and Significance: By introducing hierarchical WSI encoding and clinical-guided graph propagation, HGASurv unifies multi-scale pathology representation with topology-based clinical integration in a hierarchical granularity-aware framework. This design shows that matching representation and integration mechanisms to modality-specific granularity improves multimodal survival prediction.

title: 医疗AI下一站：从单点辅助走向多智能体协同
Rethinking selection criteria for liver transplantation in hepatocellular carcinoma: from morphology to artificial intelligence.
source: PubMed · Expert review of gastroenterology & hepatology
desc: [Expert review of gastroenterology & hepatology] Liver transplantation (LT) is a uniquely curative treatment for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), as it removes both the tumor and the underlying cirrhotic liver. However, organ scarcity makes candidate selection a central clinical and ethical issue. Over the past three decades, selection has evolved from simple morphologic thresholds toward increasingly multidimensional models of oncologic risk. This review examines the evolution of selection criteria for LT in HCC, from the Milan criteria and subsequent morphology-based expansions to models incorporating tumor biology, serum biomarkers, treatment response, waiting-list dynamics, and artificial intelligence. The literature discussed includes landmark morphologic criteria, AFP-based models, PIVKA-II and AFP-L3 integration, downstaging strategies, dynamic scores such as TRAIN and NYCA, and machine-learning models including MoRAL-AI, TRIUMPH, and TRAIN-AI. The field is moving from categorical eligibility rules toward individualized, continuous risk estimation. Future selection should not aim merely to expand transplant access, but to identify patients most likely to achieve durable oncologic benefit. Artificial intelligence, radiomics, liquid biopsy, and multi-omic profiling may refine risk prediction, but their clinical adoption will require prospective validation, transparency, calibration, transportability, and integration into allocation systems.

title: TIM: Temporal Decoupling with Iterative Mutual-Refinement Model for Longitudinal Radiology Report Generation
desc: Automatic radiology report generation (RRG) aims to translate medical images into diagnostic text, reducing radiologists' workload and standardizing clinical documentation. Nonetheless, existing approaches mainly focus on single-timepoint analysis and fail to capture temporal disease evolution across longitudinal examinations. While recent longitudinal RRG (LRRG) approaches incorporate historical data, they often combine images from different time points within a single representation space, leading to blurred semantics and inconsistent temporal reasoning. In this work, we propose a Temporal Decoupling with Iterative Mutual-Refinement Model (TIM), a two-stage framework that explicitly decouples spatial pathology from temporal progression and iteratively refines reports through mutual feedback. Stage I performs temporal-decoupled representation learning, separating temporal evolution patterns from disease-specific features and generating radiology reports for both prior and current studies. Stage II introduces a mutual report refinement mechanism that identifies diagnostic inconsistencies within prior reports and iteratively rectifies both prior and current reports through error-sensitive feedback. Experiments on the Longitudinal-MIMIC dataset demonstrate that TIM surpasses existing single-image and longitudinal baselines, achieving new state-of-the-art performance across both language and clinical metrics. Code is available at https://github.com/yihengd/TIM.
