[Clinical reasoning in the age of artificial intelligence: the urgent need for formal education].
desc: [Harefuah] Clinical reasoning remains the cornerstone of medical practice, yet unlike anatomy or physiology, medical curricula rarely teach it explicitly. This omission has significant consequences, as diagnostic errors account for up to 15% of adverse events in healthcare. Theoretical models such as Dual Process Theory (System 1 intuitive vs. System 2 analytical reasoning), illness scripts, and metacognition highlight both the strengths and vulnerabilities of clinical cognition. The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into clinical practice intensifies the need for structured reasoning education. While large language models demonstrate impressive diagnostic capabilities, risks such as automation bias and AI confabulations threaten safe decision-making. Consequently, this review calls for a paradigm shift: clinical reasoning must become a formal, longitudinal core subject across all stages of medical education. In the AI era, clinical reasoning is not diminished; it is indispensable.

title: HypTI: Hyperbolic Geometry-Aware Multimodal Feature Fusion Framework for Dementia Detection Based on Tabular-Image Data
desc: AI-assisted dementia detection usually requires multimodal fusion of diverse data, such as clinical tabular assessments and neuroimaging data. However, most existing approaches perform feature fusion in Euclidean space. This overlooks the geometric structure of representation, including hierarchical organization in clinical assessments and multi-scale anatomical patterns in neuroimaging data. Recent studies have proved hyperbolic space provides a natural geometry for modelling hierarchical and multi-scale structures due to its exponentially expanding space. Motivated by these, we propose HypTI, a hyperbolic geometry-aware multimodal fusion framework for dementia detection based on clinical tabular assessments and MRI scans. HypTI extends hyperbolic representation learning to an underexplored tabular-MRI setting, jointly modelling clinical tabular, MRI scans, and cross-modal interactions in hyperbolic space. Specifically, clinical tabular variables are represented through learnable Lorentz prototypes to capture hierarchical relationships among assessments, while MRI scans are encoded using ROI-guided multi-scale representation learning to capture anatomical patterns across brain regions and spatial scales in Lorentz space. The multimodal representations are integrated through an adaptive fusion module generates subject-specific scale and shift coefficients to dynamically modulate and integrate the multimodal embeddings, enabling effective patient-level tabular-image representation learning for dementia detection. Experiments on OASIS-3 dataset show that the proposed framework achieves strong performance compared with representative approaches.

Evaluating the Automated Extraction of Radiation Oncology Trial Data at Scale from the ClinicalTrials.gov Database Using a Large Language Model.
desc: [Oncology] Background The rapid growth of biomedical publishing in radiation oncology has created a need for automated methods to extract structured information from unstructured text. Large language models (LLMs) show promise in biomedical natural language processing, but their use for clinical trial data curation remains to be systematically evaluated. Methods We evaluated an LLM-based extraction system for radiation oncology trials on ClinicalTrials.gov. Forty-five classification questions spanning variables such as trial design, tumor type, stage, radiotherapy modality, systemic therapy, and outcomes were implemented using the data-element-extractor Python library with three open-source LLMs (GPT-OSS-20B, GPT-OSS-120B, and Qwen-3.6-27B). A manually curated ground-truth of 94 trials was used for performance evaluation based on accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. Results Qwen-3.6-27B achieved the highest overall accuracy of 92.0% across all questions. For the 39 Boolean questions, it demonstrated 93.0% accuracy, 81.6% precision, 83.7% recall, and an F1-score of 82.6%, with 23 Boolean questions achieving an F1-score ≥80.0%. Three numerical questions reached accuracy ≥80.0%. Applied to the full dataset, the system characterized the clinical landscape of radiotherapy trials, detailing the prevalence of advanced techniques (e.g., 13.7% SBRT) and the integration of systemic agents, including chemotherapy (57.3%) and immunotherapy (26.1%). Conclusion LLM-based extraction can enable accurate, scalable curation of radiotherapy trial data. While challenges remain with complex categorical or numerical variables, open-source LLMs can serve as effective components of transparent, auditable clinical research pipelines.

title: Privacy-Preserving Personalized Federated Learning (PPP-FL) for Medical Imaging
desc: Federated learning (FL) is a distributed machine learning paradigm that reduces transmission costs, mitigates cross-border data sharing restrictions, and enhances privacy by keeping raw data on local devices. Clients in FL systems train local models and share only updates, which are aggregated by a central server. While this setup limits direct data exposure, FL remains vulnerable to privacy attacks. Existing attack and defense strategies have largely been developed for centralized systems, and adapting them to FL introduces new challenges due to its unique architecture and training workflow. In this work, we first propose a model inversion attack on FL systems using Deep Convolutional Generative Adversarial Networks (DCGANs) in the context of large-scale medical imaging. Our method operates under realistic assumptions about the attacker's knowledge and capabilities. We then examine the effect of client-side differential privacy (DP) in mitigating privacy leakage and incorporate personalized FL to improve model performance under DP settings. Experiments on the Brain MRI ND-5 dataset show that DCGAN-based attacks can reconstruct semantically meaningful synthetic images, revealing significant risks to the privacy of training data. Applying DP reduces attack success but introduces an accuracy trade-off, which is further overcome by personalized FL at each client side. We also evaluate how different aggregation algorithms affect both attack vulnerability and defense effectiveness, underscoring the critical role of aggregation strategies. The proposed attack-and-defense framework is model-agnostic and applicable to a wide range of FL-based systems.

title: Overuse and False Restraint in Large Language Model Recommendations for Choosing Wisely Scenarios.
desc: [Annals of internal medicine] The Choosing Wisely initiative made recommendations where screening, testing, or treatment may be overused, with caveats around appropriate use. Clinicians are increasingly using large language models (LLMs). To evaluate whether commercial LLMs appropriately call for restraint or action from scenarios based on Choosing Wisely recommendations. Benchmark evaluation. Fifteen Choosing Wisely recommendations were used to develop 225 scenarios (per recommendation, 10 in which restraint was appropriate and 5 in which action was appropriate). Six commercial LLMs (3 runs each) generated 4050 responses to the 225 scenarios, using a prompt from the clinician perspective. Production application programming interfaces of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google from February to March 2026. No human participants were involved. Co-primary outcomes were the overuse rate (endorsing action when restraint was appropriate) and the false restraint rate (withholding an appropriate action). The rate of LLM-recommended overuse was 5.4% (95% CI, 0.6% to 12.2%); LLMs did not recommend overuse in 8 of 15 recommendations. Two recommendations accounted for most LLM-recommended overuse: thyroid ultrasound for an incidental subcentimeter nodule (overuse recommended in 42.8% of LLM responses) and routine electrocardiography in low-risk adults (overuse recommended in 28.3% of LLM responses). The LLMs recommended overuse in 0.6% to 3.3% of responses for the remaining 5 recommendations. False restraint was rare (0.6% [CI, 0.1% to 1.2%]), was absent for 11 of 15 recommendations, and was highest for prostate-specific antigen screening (3.3%). Single prompts without follow-up; a benchmark rather than real-world use; responses classified by LLM judge with physician adjudication. Findings may not extend to consumer-facing use. The LLMs rarely withheld recommendations for treatment when it was appropriate. Overuse was concentrated in 2 recommendations. None.

title: MoSAIK: Motion Search with Artificial Intelligence in K-space
desc: Object: Motion artefacts remain a major limitation of routine two-dimensional T2-weighted turbo spin-echo (TSE) brain MRI, reducing diagnostic confidence and often necessitating repeated acquisitions. MoSAIK (Motion Search with AI in K-space) retrospectively estimates in-plane rigid-body motion directly from standard multi-coil TSE k-space. Without a motion-free reference, external navigators, or additional acquisitions, MoSAIK infers motion from k-space self-consistency violations and incorporates predicted parameters into model-based, motion-aware reconstruction rather than synthesizing corrected images. Materials and Methods: Selected complex coil data were represented as log-magnitude and phase channels. A decoupled convolutional embedding and Transformer encoder estimated phase-encoding-line-indexed rotation and two-dimensional translations. Training used motion-free clinical acquisitions with simulated motion; four held-out subjects were evaluated. Component-wise errors assessed estimation; SSIM and PSNR in silico and entropy focus criterion (EFC) in vivo assessed reconstruction. Results: Motion estimation errors were low for both rotation (MSE $<$ 0.2 deg$^2$) and translation (MSE $<$ 0.2 pixels$^2$), with Pearson correlations of approximately 0.96 and 0.94, respectively. In every in-vivo acquisition, more than 75% of slices showed information gain relative to uncorrected reconstructions. MoSAIK reduced visible artefacts while preserving anatomical detail. Discussion: Transformer-based k-space motion-trajectory estimation enables fast retrospective correction of standard clinical TSE brain MRI.

title: Development of a Natural Language Processing Algorithm to Aid Creation of a Surgical Spine Database.
source: PubMed · The spine journal : official journal of the North American Spine Society
desc: [The spine journal : official journal of the North American Spine Society] Manual effort required for feature extraction from operative reports can be time-intensive, inaccurate, and costly. Develop a natural language processing (NLP) algorithm for surgical spine database creation and validate performance against human reviewers with varying clinical experience. Retrospective study at a tertiary academic institution from 2008-2024. Operative spinal cases on adult patients from 22,951 spinal operative reports. Primary outcome was accuracy in operated spinal level classification. Secondary outcomes include clinical diagnoses, operative procedures, and additional surgical detail classification. A rule-based NLP algorithm was developed and validated on a random sample of 100 operative reports. Performance of the NLP algorithm and human reviewers was assessed against a reference standard. An a priori acceptability threshold was set at 0.90 for agreement, kappa, and F1. Time required for chart review/processing were also assessed for the NLP algorithm and human reviewers. The NLP algorithm matched the reference standard on operated spinal levels (Percent Agreement=93%; Kappa=0.98; F1=0.98), which outperformed human reviewers in clinical training. Performance on procedural and diagnostic feature extraction did not meet the accepted threshold but largely outperformed human validators in clinical training. NLP algorithm computation time averaged speed of 1,039 reports per minute, compared to the fastest median time of 1 minute per operative report for human chart reviewers. The NLP algorithm can accurately and reliably extract operated spinal levels from high volumes of operative reports. However, classification of diagnosis, operative procedures, and additional surgical procedures were not sufficient for practical implementation.

title: Cross-disorder Learning of Imaging-derived Joint Mophometric Markers in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's Diseases
desc: As two most prevalent neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs), Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD) shared commonalities both in symptomology and pathophysiology. However, to what extent and in what way these two distinct disorders overlap remain underexplored. In this study, we propose an explicit, interpretable and spatially adaptive transfer learning framework to elucidate the morphometric biomarkers linked to AD and PD. We applied such high-dimensional machine learning model to two most popular open-source neuroimaging datasets, i.e., Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) and Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI). On the one hand, our cross-disorder classifier revealed neuro-anatomical alteration patterns well aligning with previous neuroimaging research findings and underscoring patients' clinical presentations. On the other hand, the spatially adaptive trained classifier using shared prior achieved statistically superior diagnostic performance compared to respective individual models, which further highlights the cross-disorder framework's efficacy on modeling limited-size datasets across disease domains.

title: A Survey of Computational Color Constancy: Approaches and Emerging Applications in Medical Imaging.
source: PubMed · Journal of imaging informatics in medicine
desc: [Journal of imaging informatics in medicine] As the evening sets in and natural light fades to artificial light, it is remarkable how the colors around us still appear nearly the same. This phenomenon, known as color constancy, allows us to perceive relatively stable colors even as lighting conditions change. In the field of computer vision, replicating this human ability is the key to performing tasks such as recognizing objects and understanding scenes. This review examines two main approaches to tackle the challenge of computational color constancy: traditional static methods that rely on a set of assumptions about lighting and scene conditions, and newer learning-based methods that use models trained to estimate lighting directly from images. We look at how these techniques have evolved, from foundational methods like the gray-world assumption, which work within certain limitations, to modern deep learning techniques that can interpret lighting in more dynamic ways. The datasets, metrics, and reported results of the surveyed studies are consolidated into two comparative tables, providing a structured overview of the methods discussed. Together, these comparisons offer a broad perspective on how computational color constancy has developed and where it is headed, with particular emphasis on its applications in medical imaging.

title: Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?
desc: Multi-agent LLM systems improve performance on clinical tasks, and that improvement is often read as evidence of a more trustworthy system. However, the two are not the same claim. A clinician acts on the stated reasoning and not only on the conclusion, so whether collaboration reduces hallucination, and what decides when it does, has to be measured in the reasoning too. Yet most evaluations score only the final answer. We evaluate four systems (a single-LLM baseline and three multi-agent topologies) across four models and three clinical tasks, scoring hallucination, under a factuality and faithfulness taxonomy, inside the rationale each system generates and reporting it alongside the task metric. We report that collaboration buys task performance but not lower hallucination as a rule, and no topology is reliably better than another. The effect differs by model: of the $36$ model--system--task comparisons, $12$ are large enough to resolve --- four decreases and eight increases, with no model on both sides. What sets the level, and the direction of any change, is the model rather than the topology or the number of agents. A self-correction experiment is consistent with this: shown its own flagged errors, every model except Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct reduces hallucination; the one model for which collaboration lowers hallucination gains the most, and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, the model whose hallucination it amplifies most, does not reduce its hallucination at all. We find that collaboration redistributes what its models can already do; it does not supply what they cannot.

title: Artificial Intelligence Use Among Health Care Professionals in the United States and United Kingdom: Cross-National Survey.
desc: [JMIR formative research] This cross-sectional study examined AI use among 524 health care professionals in the United States and United Kingdom, focusing on current applications, access, barriers, and factors that could support adoption. AI use was common but varied across professional and national contexts, with findings highlighting the importance of evidence, organizational guidance, training, privacy safeguards, and integration into clinical workflows for responsible adoption.

title: 3D Diffusion Models for Medical Imaging
desc: Generative deep learning methods such as Variational Autoencoders, Generative Adversarial Networks or Diffusion Models have achieved remarkable results in image synthesis. In particular, Diffusion Models have demonstrated superior image fidelity and sample diversity compared to other approaches on standard benchmarks, while also offering more flexible training dynamics as evidenced both in natural image domains and in medical applications. In medical imaging including Computed Tomography, Magnetic Resonance Imaging or Positron Emission Tomography, such models have various important use-cases including data augmentation, domain transfer, image reconstruction, inpainting, image augmentation and artifact correction. Further, generated images can be conditioned on patient characteristics, medical reports, segmentation masks or other images. Specific challenges arise due to the 3D volumetric nature of medical images, which translate to substantial demands in terms of memory, compute, and training data. This article provides a comparative overview of 3D Diffusion Models which have been developed for medical images, with a focus on current performance, limitations, and an outlook for future work.

title: Hair Segmentation and Skin Characterization on Macroscopic Dermatological Images for Laser Treatment Parameterization.
source: PubMed · Journal of imaging informatics in medicine
desc: [Journal of imaging informatics in medicine] Current light-based devices, such as laser hair removal, intense pulsed light (IPL), vascular laser therapy, and dermatologic phototherapy, are widely used in clinical dermatology but rely heavily on subjective manual parameterization or uncalibrated point-based colorimeters. To overcome these limitations, this work presents a unified system for hair segmentation and skin characterization in macroscopic dermatological images. Unlike most existing literature that relies on dermoscopic datasets captured under highly controlled conditions, our approach is specifically designed for macroscopic images that replicate real clinical laser treatments. The proposed pipeline integrates a custom-trained variant of the YOLOv9 deep learning architecture for instance segmentation and classical image processing within a single workflow to extract objective skin and hair parameters such as phototype, hair density, color, and thickness. A color calibration stage using spectrophotometric measurements ensures accurate feature estimation regardless of illumination conditions. Experimental results show competitive segmentation metrics (mAP@50 ≈ 0.80) on a custom dataset featuring short, shaved hairs, typical of pre-treatment scenarios. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed pipeline in providing the objective, foundational skin and hair features required for future automated laser parameterization, paving the way for its extension to broader light-based medical therapies.

title: LeakBench: Auditing Reward Hacking through Prediction-Time Leakage in Clinical Modeling Agents
desc: Autonomous clinical-modeling agents can optimize predictive performance while violating conditions that make a model usable. We introduce LeakBench, an executable, guideline-derived audit suite that tests agent decisions for prediction-time leakage, calibration, site-level evaluation, support awareness, and decision-curve net benefit. LeakBench combines a synthetic task with known failure structure and two real-data settings: MIMIC-IV (430k admissions) and governed multi-hospital inpatient record front-page (MHFP) data. Our primary analysis uses reward hacking descriptively, without attributing intent: an agent selects prediction-time-invalid inputs because they improve its validation reward. A deterministic optimizer and every evaluated unconstrained local-model configuration select a fatal leaking feature. In fully logged September 2026 A/B runs, DeepSeek Flash and GPT-6-astra each leak in 10/10 unconstrained runs and 0/10 runs with an explicit admission-time constraint. This contrast is version-sensitive: a blinded Claude/Fable-5.1 chat run does not leak in either condition, while explicit-constraint violations appear only in a historical August 2026 slice lacking raw trajectories. Replacing AUROC with AUPRC does not remove leakage selection. Renaming or disguising the leaking inputs changes neither selection nor provenance-based detection; a name-based filter fails. A deterministic provenance verifier-in-loop removes the leak, making the LLM repair loop defense-in-depth. Specific verifier feedback clears fatal leakage in a hosted agent, and a three-seed ablation finds principle-only feedback clears decision-level defects, though these mitigation results are limited. LeakBench treats trustworthy clinical prediction as a property of an agent's modeling process, not merely its score; it is an audit testbed with known-failure controls, not yet an expert-validated benchmark.

title: Predicting trail-making test performance using 7-Tesla structural cerebral MRI.
desc: [Translational psychiatry] Psychopharmaceutical therapy has seen a lack of improvement in efficacy, highlighting the need for a more individualized treatment approach that optimally leverages pharmaceutical effects. To achieve this, it is necessary to identify factors that can predict psychological attributes and treatment outcomes. We hypothesize that brain morphology may serve as a predictor of performance in psychological tests. A 7-Tesla-MRI system was used to measure 74 transdiagnostic patients and 41 healthy controls. Values for grey matter volume (GMV), cortical thickness and gyrification based on the Schaefer 100 Atlas for parcellation were determined. Using this morphological data, performance in a Trail-Making Test (TMT) - A and B was predicted with the help of a deep learning model. A SHAP analysis was conducted to identify the key variables important for the model. The accuracy in predicting TMT performance was very good at 0.795. The most decisive feature influencing predictions was gyrification. Areas indicating inter-group differences were focused in the frontal cortex, as well as in temporal and parietal regions. Morphological characteristics can predict test performance with high accuracy. These results support the implementation of a transdiagnostic approach in clinical practice to better address the underlying pathophysiology. Symptom prediction based on neuroimaging data appears to be an achievable goal.

title: PCXR-Copilot: Device-aware pediatric chest radiographic analysis with segmentation, suppression, and edema-related cues
desc: Patients admitted to pediatric ICU and cardiac ICU often require intensive perioperative support and frequent chest radiography to monitor support devices, extravascular lung water, and body-wall edema. Radiographic interpretation and analysis is often difficult due to superimposed anatomic and iatrogenic structures that obscure clinically relevant signals. While deep learning can provide decision support, translation to pediatric radiographs is still limited by high device burden and scarcity of pediatric datasets with clinically grounded device annotations. To address this gap, we first introduce PediaDeviceSeg-1K, a curated dataset of 1,000 anterior-posterior radiographs of pediatric CICU patients with clinically grounded, fine-grained annotations of common ICU devices. To our best knowledge, this is the first publicly available pediatric CICU CXR resource with clinically grounded device annotations for device-focused benchmarking. Building on PediaDeviceSeg-1K, we further present PCXR-Copilot, a device-aware pipeline that outputs lung and device masks, optional device-suppressed views, and edema-related visualization maps and scalar indices. The full pipeline has been integrated and runs in real time within the TWIST platform at Boston Children's Hospital, demonstrating feasibility for real-world clinical deployment.

title: Advancing the use of artificial intelligence in psychiatry: The need for international collaboration.
source: PubMed · European psychiatry : the journal of the Association of European Psychiatrists
desc: [European psychiatry : the journal of the Association of European Psychiatrists] Challenging macrotrends in recent decades have characterised population mental health across the globe, with apparent deterioration in adolescent mental health, as well as underfunded, inequitable, and inefficient psychiatric care systems [1]. Unnecessary delays to treatment are widespread, with systemic difficulties, such as clinician burnout, a dearth of funding, and staff shortages, negatively impacting mental health care across Europe and beyond [2]. With limited clinician time and resources available, new methods for improving mental health care are an urgent priority. Digital technologies, and particularly recent advances in the capabilities of artificial intelligence (AI), offer potential to address some of these challenges, thereby transforming approaches to mental health care.

title: Multimodal-Conditioned Latent Diffusion Models for Spatiotemporal Brain MRI Forecasting
desc: Spatiotemporal forecasting of 3D anatomical changes is a critical generative vision challenge for modeling Alzheimer's Disease (AD) progression. While brain MRI forecasting from single-modality data has advanced, other key complementary multimodal biomarkers remain underutilized. In this work, we propose the Multimodal-Conditioned Latent Diffusion Model (MC-LDM), a novel framework for patient-specific brain MRI synthesis. MC-LDM leverages multimodal biomarkers---MRI, tau-PET, Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR), and APOE4---during training, but relies only on baseline MRI, APOE4, and patient metadata at inference, reflecting realistic clinical availability. Our contributions are threefold: (1) a Latent Diffusion Model (LDM) fine-tuned via Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) for data-efficient learning; (2) a multimodal conditioning that integrates molecular and clinical signals to model heterogeneous disease trajectories; and (3) auxiliary predictors estimating unobserved multimodal biomarkers from MRI features and patient covariates to condition the diffusion model, removing the need for these assessments at inference. Trained on 1,355 visits from 852 subjects in the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), MC-LDM reduces average regional volumetric MAE by 18% over the second-best baseline on an independent test set of 664 visits. To our knowledge, MC-LDM represents the first diffusion-based framework to leverage multimodal priors for MRI forecasting. This conceptual advancement enables patient-specific trajectory generation that captures aspects of AD heterogeneity not observable from structural anatomy alone, bridging the gap between rich multimodal supervision and the strict constraints of routine clinical deployment. Code is available at: https://github.com/antonioscardace/MC-LDM.

title: A Drone-Integrated Artificial Intelligence-Based System for Mass-Casualty Triage and Remote Monitoring.
desc: [Prehospital and disaster medicine] Triage and data transfer are critical to the medical management of mass-casualty incidents (MCIs). However, the chaotic nature of such events makes it difficult to classify casualties according to structured triage protocols. Furthermore, even when triage is implemented effectively, communication disruptions between the incident scene and dispatch centers can hinder response operations. The aim of this study was to present a drone-integrated system that enables non-contact vital sign measurement, remote triage, and real-time data transmission during MCIs. The system development process involved three steps: (1) developing the Vital-Sign Measurement Module; (2) developing the Triage Decision Support Module; and (3) developing the User Interfaces and Data Transmission Module to enable information transmission between dispatch centers and response teams. Within the Vital-Sign Measurement Module, heart rate (HR), respiratory rate (RR), oxygen saturation (SpO2), and body temperature (BT) measurement algorithms were developed using the following techniques, respectively: video-based photoplethysmography (vPPG), analysis of thermal temperature fluctuations around the nose, a regression-based neural network approach, and heat maps and thermal thresholding. A pilot study was conducted under controlled indoor conditions to evaluate the accuracy of these algorithms. The system can measure vital signs by processing drone-captured images, can provide triage decision support, and can transmit victims' locations, vital signs, and triage categories to response teams and dispatch centers via dedicated user interfaces. A pilot evaluation of the Vital-Sign Measurement Module showed that the relative accuracy rate of the non-contact vital-sign measurement algorithms ranged from 86% to 99%. The system provides an innovative approach to improving medical response management in MCIs by enabling remote triage and monitoring. Its non-contact vital sign measurement, triage decision support, and near real-time data transmission capabilities provide an infrastructure that can contribute to faster response and improved operational coordination. However, further field trials and development are required to improve the robustness of the vital-sign measurement algorithms to motion, to improve their adaptability to changing environmental conditions, and to maintain high accuracy despite individual differences.

title: CoRe-WM: Conditioned Response-State World Modeling for Longitudinal Treatment-Response Prediction in Breast DCE-MRI
desc: Pathologic complete response (pCR) after neoadjuvant chemotherapy is a key prognostic indicator in aggressive breast cancer, yet existing prediction approaches either rely on pretreatment imaging alone, missing the patient's evolving response, or optimize multi-visit classifiers under direct outcome supervision, coupling representation learning with the clinical endpoint. We formulate longitudinal pCR prediction as a world-modeling problem and propose Conditioned Response-state World Modeling (CoRe-WM), which learns a latent state-transition model that predicts the next imaging state from the observed sequence. The transition function is conditioned on patient clinical profile and assigned therapy through additive shift and feature-wise modulation, enabling patient- and treatment-specific dynamics. A Factorized Response State pathway further decouples treatment-response dynamics from imaging appearance by encoding the structural prior that response manifests primarily in lesion morphology. After pretraining, all parameters are frozen and a linear readout predicts pCR at each clinical decision point. We evaluate CoRe-WM on I-SPY2 under five-fold cross-validation and assess cross-cohort transfer on I-SPY1. CoRe-WM achieves the highest discrimination among all evaluated methods at every prospective decision point, and demonstrates robust cross-cohort transfer. Ablation studies identify patient-profile conditioning and the factorized response pathway as the principal contributors. These results establish world-model-based representation learning as a promising framework for outcome prediction in oncology and beyond.

title: [Maximum limb reconstruction: concept and implementation strategies].
source: PubMed · Zhongguo xiu fu chong jian wai ke za zhi = Zhongguo xiufu chongjian waike zazhi = Chinese journal of reparative and reconstructive surgery
desc: [Zhongguo xiu fu chong jian wai ke za zhi = Zhongguo xiufu chongjian waike zazhi = Chinese journal of reparative and reconstructive surgery] Thanks to the rapid development of modern science and medicine, limb reconstruction can and should be taken to the next level. The author proposes the concept of "maximum limb reconstruction", which pursues not merely function but the maximal normalization of structure, morphology, and function, leveraging advances in prosthetics, artificial intelligence, and exoskeleton technology to enhance limb preservation. For the three pathological states-defect, infection, and deformity-sequential strategies are outlined: ① mutilating injuries are managed in three phases (early revascularization, mid-term wound coverage and infection control, late length restoration and functional reconstruction); ② osteomyelitis treatment must prioritize radical debridement over reconstructive techniques; ③ severe deformities require active limb salvage treatment, long-term follow-up, and recognition of natural remodeling potential. Ultimately, limb reconstruction surgeons should integrate modern technology with holistic patient needs-physical, psychological, and sexual-to continuously improve outcomes, recognizing that the native limb, however imperfect, holds irreplaceable value for human identity and well-being.

title: PACE-MoE: Adaptive Domain Sampling and Domain-Specific LoRA for Medical Visual Grounding
desc: Medical visual grounding requires models to align clinical descriptions with spatial evidence across heterogeneous imaging domains. However, existing multi-domain post-training strategies typically rely on fixed domain sampling and shared parameter updates, overlooking the need to adapt both which domains receive training and where their updates are applied. To address this issue, we propose PACE-MoE, a policy-guided framework that jointly performs adaptive domain sampling and domain-specific adaptation for medical visual grounding. PACE dynamically assesses the training value of each imaging domain from current-policy feedback and progressively adjusts domain coverage through domain admission, replay, and final all-domain balancing. Meanwhile, domain-specific LoRA adapters route updates to the corresponding imaging domains while preserving the pretrained backbone and visual encoder. This coordinated design aligns training-data allocation with parameter adaptation without modifying the original reward formulation or Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) objective. Experiments across seven medical imaging domains show that PACE-MoE consistently improves grounding performance over fixed-domain training, achieving a 3.64% relative improvement in mean box IoU over the Vanilla baseline. Under matched domain-specific adapter architectures, adaptive sampling alone further improves mean box IoU by 2.07%, demonstrating the benefit of policy-guided domain allocation. These results establish coordinated data-parameter routing as an effective strategy for multi-domain medical visual grounding.

title: Decoding morality through EEG with ML: rigour, risks, and the road ahead.
desc: [Cognitive neurodynamics] The quest to decode morality through electroencephalography (EEG) with machine learning (ML) is as much about confronting the risks of opaque algorithms as it is about harnessing their scientific promise. This systematic review synthesises 17 empirical studies published between 2018 and 2025 that employed ML or deep learning (DL) approaches to EEG data within moral cognition paradigms. Following PRISMA guidelines, studies were identified across four electronic databases and categorised into eight experimental paradigms spanning three thematic branches: Evaluation, Emotion, and Prosociality. The Ultimatum Game was the most frequently applied paradigm (n = 6), while classical ML approaches dominated methodological choices, accounting for 65% of the included studies. Despite the growing interest in DL, interpretability was inconsistently addressed, with Explainable Artificial Intelligence methods applied in only one of the six DL studies and in just two of the 17 included studies overall. This review highlights three pressing methodological gaps: the need for multimodal fusion to capture richer neural signals, the integration of transfer learning to enhance generalisability, and the adoption of standardised interpretability reporting to ensure transparency. We argue that ML offers a scientifically rigorous pathway for advancing EEG-based moral cognition research, but only when models are robustly validated and their outputs rendered explainable. Without these safeguards, the promise of decoding morality risks being undermined by opaque algorithms and methodological blind spots. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s11571-026-10559-4.

title: SCODEL: Shared Canonical Ontology Definitions for Food Entity Linking and Ontology-Grounded Recipe Knowledge Graphs
desc: Identifying recipe entities and linking them to ontology concepts is fundamental for semantic recipe understanding. However, food mentions in recipes are often ambiguous, context-dependent, and lexically diverse, making ontology entity linking (EL) challenging. We propose SCODEL, a streamlined, model-agnostic approach based on a central idea: contextual food mentions and ontology concepts that refer to the same entity should learn the same canonical ontology-oriented definition. SCODEL uses these shared definitions as a semantic normalisation layer, providing complementary semantic information to existing EL models without requiring a new linking architecture. We further introduce ReciLinkD, the first benchmark for contextual food ontology entity linking in recipes. Experiments show that SCODEL consistently improves three modular EL models (ReFinED, GSM-EL, and BLINK): SCODEL x BLINK achieves the highest Hit@1 on seen concepts (88.33%), while SCODEL x GSM-EL achieves the highest Hit@1 on unseen concepts (83.15%), outperforming the strongest large language model (LLM) based EL baseline in each setting. Experiments on a biomedical ontology benchmark further demonstrate that SCODEL generalises beyond the food domain. Finally, we use SCODEL to ground food mentions at scale and construct an ontology-grounded recipe knowledge graph, demonstrating its utility for ontology-aware recipe retrieval and corpus-level food analysis.

title: Function-based Deep Learning Autoencoder for Passive Shimming in a Portable MRI Magnet with Enhanced Field Homogeneity.
source: PubMed · IEEE transactions on bio-medical engineering
desc: [IEEE transactions on bio-medical engineering] High-field magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) offers excellent sensitivity and spatial resolution, yet its substantial cost and limited mobility restrict deployment in decentralized or resource-constrained environments. Portable MRI systems offer a complementary imaging modality to high-field MRI, but their performance depends critically on the uniformity of the main magnetic field (B0). Passive shimming, achieved by placing ferromagnetic materials within the magnet bore, is widely used to correct spatial field variations. Existing optimization strategies- including linear programming and evolutionary algorithms-can improve B homogeneity, but often struggle to achieve an effective trade-off among field strength, uniformity, and shim mass. To address this challenge, a function-based deep learning autoencoder (FDLAE) is proposed to optimize the spatial distribution of passive shims. The framework operates without a precompiled dataset and performs online self-supervised learning to iteratively refine the shim configuration. This approach improves B0 homogeneity from 4873 ppm to 547 ppm (parts per million) and increases the average field strength from 80.402 mT to 80.948 mT. Compared with linear programming (LP), it achieved lower inhomogeneity, reduced the shim mass by 0.29 kg, and shortened the optimization time from approximately 1.2 to 0.5 h. MRiLab simulations also showed a reduction in image NRMSE from 0.889 to 0.543. Relative to genetic-algorithm-based shimming, the resulting field uniformity is improved by nearly a factor of five. These results demonstrate that FDLAE may provide an efficient and comparatively robust passive-shimming approach for portable MRI magnets.

title: DART: Scaling a Shape Representation Across Anatomical Classes and Imaging Modalities
desc: Current state-of-the-art segmentation models still produce anatomically implausible shapes, such as broken vessels and fragmented glands, on the structures that are hardest to segment. Learned shape representations capture what structures look like and can help correct these errors, but most cover a fixed set of anatomical classes. Extending this coverage across classes and imaging modalities is costly because it often requires new voxel-level annotations. We propose Diffusion for Anatomical Reshaping with Text (DART), which learns a shared shape representation from segmentation probabilities. It uses anatomical descriptions to correct these probabilities without receiving medical images. Across 13 public benchmarks, absolute Dice gains reach 31% for individual gallbladder cases in CT and 10% for individual prostate cases in MRI. Using existing segmentation predictions, we scale a single shape representation from 50 to 377 anatomical classes without new voxel-level annotations for correction training. The shared representation also corrects four lesion classes absent from training and transfers from CT to MRI without retraining. Corrected labels also improve segmentation models, raising one model's Dice from 57.1% to 67.5%. The same pipeline supports annotations for 45,000 CT scans. These results suggest that sharing shape information within and across classes can reduce the need for new voxel-level annotations when extending segmentation to more anatomical classes and imaging modalities. The model is available at https://huggingface.co/Koushik45/DART-Seg

title: A Deep Learning Framework for Accurate lncRNA-Protein Interaction Prediction via Multi-Kernel Graph Embeddings and Self-Attention.
source: PubMed · Interdisciplinary sciences, computational life sciences
desc: [Interdisciplinary sciences, computational life sciences] Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) play a pivotal role in regulating biological processes, primarily through lncRNA-Protein Interactions (LPI), which are crucial for understanding disease mechanisms and cellular functions. While computational methods exist for predicting LPI, they suffer from suboptimal feature integration, limited generalizability, and inadequate network modeling. To address these challenges, we propose MAKGLPIN (Multi-Architecture, Multi-Kernel Graph-based LPI Network), a novel deep learning framework that integrates sequence features, structural information, and physicochemical properties of lncRNAs and proteins. MAKGLPIN employs a multi-layer Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) enhanced with a self-attention mechanism to capture complex interaction patterns, alongside a Graph Attention Network (GAT) to prioritize critical interactions while preserving long-range dependencies. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that MAKGLPIN outperforms existing methods in robustness, generalizability, and predictive precision across benchmark datasets. Our model provides a computationally efficient and biologically interpretable solution, advancing the study of LPI and their applications in disease research.

title: MMedAgent-Plus: Scaling Multimodal Medical Agents across Modalities, Tasks and Workflows
desc: Medical workflows often require multiple interdependent analyses, but existing specialist and generalist AI models are not designed to coordinate them. We introduce MMedAgent-Plus, a multimodal medical tool-use agent that combines a vision-language planner with 18 leading specialist models spanning 12 tasks and 8 modalities. Through a unified tool interface, the planner selects specialists, executes them in sequence, and synthesizes responses grounded in their outputs. The planner is instruction-tuned on 208,928 samples from 32 public medical benchmarks, covering single- and multi-tool interactions across single and multiple rounds. We separately evaluate tool orchestration, response synthesis, and end-to-end execution on held-out samples. MMedAgent-Plus achieves tool-call accuracies of 91.0%, 98.1%, and 80.7% in single-tool multi-round, multi-tool multi-round, and multi-tool single-round settings, respectively. Given correct tool outputs, MMedAgent-Plus achieves scores of 14.4-14.8 out of 15 for faithfulness, completeness, and conciseness across 600 evaluation samples. In end-to-end execution without pre-supplied tool outputs, MMedAgent-Plus correctly invokes the required specialist in 90.6% of 350 evaluation cases spanning seven tasks. Its final-answer accuracy reaches 0.98, matching the dedicated leading specialist and exceeding the strongest baseline (0.28).

title: A blessing or a curse? The impact of artificial intelligence innovation on corporate energy efficiency.
desc: [Journal of environmental management] This study examines how artificial intelligence (AI) innovation influences corporate energy efficiency and the underlying mechanisms. We develop a general equilibrium model incorporating energy input and endogenous AI technology to explain how AI innovation improves energy efficiency through production process optimization. Using a deep-learning-based text identification, we develop a firm-level measure of AI innovation for Chinese listed companies over the period 2008-2022. Our empirical results show that AI innovation significantly improves corporate energy efficiency, while the mechanism analysis provides evidence consistent with production process optimization as an important transmission channel. This positive effect is stronger among firms operating in key technological sectors and capital-intensive industries. Further, we find that disruptive AI innovation produces a larger effect than general AI innovation. We also document that local governments' attention to AI development and intra-firm data sharing strengthen the energy-efficiency gains associated with AI innovation. This study contributes to research on digital innovation and firm sustainability by showing how AI-driven innovation translates into efficiency-enhancing outcomes through organizational and data-governance mechanisms.

title: Discrete Neural Interlingua for Ontology-Agnostic EHR Modeling
desc: EHR foundation models promise scalable clinical prediction across health systems, yet their deployment is constrained by a tokenization bottleneck. The same clinical concept can appear as different ontology codes, local identifiers, synonyms, or free-text descriptions, which standard EHR tokenizers treat as unrelated symbols. A model trained on MIMIC-III with a closed-vocabulary tokenizer can use only 13% of eICU events. We introduce MEDIATOR, a discrete ontology-agnostic tokenizer that maps any clinical concept expressed as text into a shared vector-quantized codebook, turning EHR harmonization into open-vocabulary tokenization without manual mappings or a fixed vocabulary. Trained with synonym supervision and guided by enriched concept descriptions, code co-occurrence, and relation graphs, MEDIATOR collapses equivalent expressions while organizing distinct concepts in a medically meaningful discrete space. Used as the token interface of an EHR Transformer, MEDIATOR improves mean AUPRC over the strongest prior tokenizer by 4.0 points (8% relative) on 20 MIMIC-III tasks and by 8.6 points (29% relative) in zero-shot transfer to 14 eICU tasks, where it uses all events. The transfer gain combines coverage and representation, as MEDIATOR remains the best tokenizer under identical inputs (+1.0 and +1.9 points on operational and subcohort-mortality tasks). Same-encoder controls show that the text encoder drives in-domain accuracy, while the learned objectives of MEDIATOR drive transfer robustness and entity-linking quality. MEDIATOR also enables transferable attribution across hospitals.

title: Delineating neural contributions to electroencephalogram-based speech decoding.
desc: [Journal of neural engineering] Objective. Speech Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have emerged as a pivotal technology in facilitating communication for individuals with speech impairments. Utilizing electroencephalography (EEG) for noninvasive speech BCIs offers an accessible and affordable solution, potentially benefiting a broader audience. However, EEG-based speech decoding remains controversial especially for overt speech, due to difficulties in separating speech-related neural activities from myoelectric potential artifacts generated during articulation. Moreover, because paradigms for collecting covert speech data are inherently less scalable than those for overt speech, whether the neural dynamics underlying EEG-based decoding of overt speech are also present during covert speech remains an open and practically important question. Approach. Here we aim to delineate the extent of the neural contributions to EEG-based speech decoding, and the degree to which the underlying neural dynamics are shared across overt and covert speech, by employing Explainable AI techniques to a convolutional neural network predicting spoken words based on signals obtained by ultra-high-density (uhd)-EEG. Main results. We found that electrode-wise contributions to the decoding cannot be explained by their mutual information with electromyography (EMG). Furthermore, contributing periods of speech to EEG-based decoding are distinct from those to decoding solely relying on EMG. In contrast, there are significant overlaps in signal timings contributing to EEG-based decoding, regardless of vocal conditions such as overt or covert speech. Notably, the denoising process successfully enhanced the decoding contribution from electrodes within speech-related brain areas for all speech conditions. Significance. Altogether, our findings support the idea that, with appropriate preprocessing, EEG becomes a valuable tool for decoding spoken words based on underlying neural activities. .

title: What Language Adds, and at What Cost: Four Controlled Probes of Pathology Vision-Language Models
desc: Vision--language models (VLMs) promise to make computational pathology queryable and able to draft reports, but how much language adds beyond the vision backbone is unclear, because almost every system is evaluated by its developers on test sets of their own choosing. We grade published evidence by how it was produced and test four claims with controlled probes that reuse released checkpoints and public data, varying one input at a time. Report text adds prognostic signal: adding a frozen embedding of the stage-redacted report to a slide embedding raises the pooled C-index by 0.019 for progression-free interval and by 0.016 for overall survival across 1{,}633 TCGA patients, and restoring the stage statement adds nothing. Prompts add no measurable accuracy at inference: with features and pooling fixed, zero-shot classification is statistically indistinguishable from a supervised linear probe for lung and renal cancer subtyping. Slide-level question answering is barely grounded: SlideChat answers 74.82\% of SlideBench-VQA(TCGA) items correctly with the slide and 74.41\% without it, whereas its language backbone alone reaches 43.52\%. Paraphrasing leaves accuracy unchanged but flips 8--23\% of answers. Self-reported gains from agentic navigation and few-shot language priors cannot yet be attributed to language. Language thus adds real but narrow value, and we propose minimum controls that would expose these failure modes in future evaluations.

title: Integrated Biovalorization of Wastewater for Sustainable Resource Management-Circular Economy.
source: PubMed · Water environment research : a research publication of the Water Environment Federation
desc: [Water environment research : a research publication of the Water Environment Federation] Wastewater is increasingly not just seen as a burden on the environment but also a source of valuable water, nutrients, energy, carbon, and high value bioproducts for recovery. Integrated biovalorization is a promising strategy to develop conventional wastewater treatment systems into resource generating and circular ones. The review critically assesses the emerging biological platforms and integrated process configurations for wastewater biovalorization (WWB) processes such as anaerobic digestion, microbial fermentation, microalgae-bacteria systems, microbial electrochemical technologies, biofertilizer production, and wastewater biorefineries: special focus on conversion of organic carbon to volatile fatty acids, biogas, biohydrogen, biopolymer, protein, enzymes, and other value-added products, recovery of N, P, and water reclamation. The review is focused on the technological performance, resource recovery efficiency, process limitations, environmental sustainability, and commercialization opportunities of the integrated pathways. The potential of membrane technologies, nanomaterials, process intensification, and artificial intelligence and digital monitoring to enhance the process efficiency is also critically discussed. Furthermore, techno-economic analysis, life cycle effects, contaminant risks, regulatory issues, and scale-up issues are determined. Hence, future research directions towards smart, decentralized, low carbon, and commercially viable wastewater biorefineries are suggested.

title: Doubly Robust Learning of Heterogeneous Survival Treatment Effects under Time-Varying Treatments
desc: Estimating heterogeneous survival treatment effects (HSTEs) from time-to-event data under time-varying treatments is important in fields such as medicine (e.g., to decide which sequence of treatments is better in terms of survival probability). However, this task is challenging because treatment decisions, patient characteristics, and censoring probability often evolve together, requiring sequential adjustment for both treatments and censoring. Existing survival learners mostly consider a single baseline treatment assignment, while longitudinal treatment-effect learners typically assume uncensored outcomes. In this paper, we introduce a novel doubly robust learner for heterogeneous survival treatment effects under time-varying treatments and history-dependent censoring. Our framework separates the intervention window from the survival horizon, with treatment prescribed for a finite period, after which care follows its natural course. We further establish the favorable theoretical properties of Neyman-orthogonality, rate double robustness and quasi-oracle efficiency. The framework accommodates flexible machine learning models for nuisance estimation and treatment-effect regression. We evaluate our learners through several numerical experiments, demonstrating their effectiveness.

title: Critical assessment in the age of AI: challenges and opportunities for computational biology.
desc: [Bioinformatics advances] Effective computational tool development depends on our ability to measure progress with rigorous benchmarking, allowing developers to showcase advances and users to select the best of the available options. Computational biology has developed a robust infrastructure of benchmarking standards, tools/resources, and best practices to allow for rigorous and unbiased assessment. This infrastructure, however, faces growing challenges as modern artificial intelligence (AI) methods move to the forefront of computational analysis. The field has imperfectly adapted to issues problematic for benchmarking AI methods, including data entanglement, data leakage, problem-specific performance, limited theoretical guarantees, elusive ground-truth, opaque and often closed models that make reproducibility of results difficult, and dependence on impermanent data sources. In this paper, we consider how the field should tackle benchmarking in the AI era. We revisit why benchmarking matters and its history in computational biology, examine emerging AI-specific challenges, and outline practical paths forward. We argue that benchmarks should be treated as long-lived community infrastructure rather than one-off artifacts bundled with individual papers. We envision a future of critical assessment i.e. dynamic and responsive to evolving use cases, sustaining progress for advancing science in the age of AI. N/A.

title: How Robust Are Prognostic Radiomic Features? Comparing Selection Techniques on Pooled Glioblastoma Cohorts
desc: Radiomic survival studies in glioblastoma report heterogeneous prognostic features, but how much of this stems from the methodology itself is rarely examined. We analysed the association of 463 radiomic, anatomical and clinical features from pre-treatment MRI with overall survival in 705 IDH-wildtype glioblastoma patients from three public cohorts, using three techniques: a log-rank test after median split, univariate Cox regression (both Benjamini-Hochberg corrected) and an XGBoost regressor interpreted with SHAP. The log-rank test selected 99 features, Cox regression 72 and SHAP its top 20; five were selected by all three: age, a peritumoural T2 texture feature, the number of connected peritumoural mask components and two image-level intensity maxima. The two survival tests shared 51 features, about half of the SHAP top 20 were also selected by either test, and where selections overlapped, effect directions agreed. Many selections were PyRadiomics diagnostic descriptors that are not restricted to tumour voxels. Analytical pipeline choices, including ranking method, pre-filtering and descriptor handling, can substantially influence which features appear prognostic.

title: Can explainable artificial intelligence classify asthma and COPD from xenon-129 ventilation magnetic resonance imaging?
desc: [ERJ open research] Explainability-derived imaging biomarkers offer a path to uncovering functional patterns linked to structural changes, advancing 129Xe-MRI toward clinical, biomarker-driven phenotyping in asthma and COPD https://bit.ly/4fRksAa.

title: UtilityBench: Measuring Language Model Utility When Errors Have Different Costs
desc: As language models are increasingly deployed in real-world scenarios with important outcomes, the impact of their mistakes often extends far beyond what correctness can capture. In domains like medicine, a single error can lead to serious consequences and put patient safety at risk. However, mainstream evaluation protocols still treat all errors as equal, overlooking the spectrum of real-world costs. To address this, we propose a utility-based evaluation paradigm that explicitly incorporates the varying consequences of errors. Guided by this principle, we develop UtilityBench, a large-scale benchmark of 15,000 instances with verifiable answers, quantifying error severity using Best-Worst Scaling to elicit meaningful, data-driven cost estimates. These quantified utilities shape when a model should answer or abstain, guiding it to make decisions that align with the true importance of each scenario. As another merit, we introduce UtilityAUC, a metric that measures the area under the utility curve determined by a model's response ordering, thereby enabling utility preference alignment beyond error frequency. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that UtilityAUC can distinguish between models where standard accuracy and AURC fall short. Empirically, evaluating 20 state-of-the-art models, we find that greater accuracy or more advanced architectures do not reliably translate to higher UtilityAUC, highlighting a gap between problem-solving ability and responsible decision-making in language model evaluation.

title: Scalable and Interpretable Chemical Neurotoxicity Prediction via Multi-Modal Gated Fusion and ChemBERTa.
desc: [Environmental science & technology] Chemical exposure causes adverse neurological outcomes, highlighting the need for high-throughput screening of chemical neurotoxicity. However, existing computational methods rely on single-modality inputs and lack complementary molecular information to sufficiently enhance the accuracy and efficiency of neurotoxicity risk assessment. Here, we present NeuroToxPredictor, a scalable and interpretable multimodal framework built on a curated chemical neurotoxicity dataset for accurate and efficient chemical neurotoxicity prediction. It integrates graph attention networks and molecular fingerprints with ChemBERTa, a pretrained chemical language model that provides contextual encoding of SMILES. A gated fusion module adaptively weights these complementary representations according to their predictive relevance to enhance modality-specific weight allocation through a gating fusion mechanism. NeuroToxPredictor achieved competitive performance across five independent training seeds (AUC = 0.919 ± 0.004; accuracy = 0.845 ± 0.014; F1-score = 0.861 ± 0.011; recall = 0.884 ± 0.013; precision = 0.839 ± 0.024; MCC = 0.688 ± 0.028), outperforming both single-modality and reduced-modality baselines. It demonstrates strong generalizability with an AUC of 0.861, as externally validated on an independent set of 279 compounds. NeuroToxPredictor is deployed on a publicly platform (https://www.ai4environ.cn/NeuroToxPredictor), enabling an end-to-end intelligent workflow from chemical retrieval, neurotoxicity prediction, applicability-domain assessment, and large language model-assisted result interpretation.

title: Multi-scale Fusion of Fast Vision Mamba and Foundation Model Features for Patch-Level Gleason Grading in Computational Pathology
desc: Automated Gleason grading of prostate whole slide images (WSIs) enables faster and more consistent cancer risk stratification. However, it remains a challenging task due to the subtle morphological differences between grades, the severe class imbalance arising from rare patterns, and the diagnostic features that span multiple spatial scales. Pathology foundation models (FMs) extract strong patch representations but often operate at a single-scale, which limits spatial context and disproportionately affects classes that depend on broader context. The challenge of fusing multiple scales and complementary models, with minimal data and computational resources, remains unresolved. We propose a multi-scale classifier built on state-space models. Our method combines two complementary feature sources: a frozen foundation model, and a lightweight FastVim, pre-trained on ImageNet and distilled from the foundation model, that reads the raw image crops. At each scale, a Mamba model encodes the features from both sources with linear-time spatial context, and a jointly trained head fuses the encoded representations into one prediction. On the PANDA dataset, our method reaches macro F1 of 0.894 and Gleason 5 F1 of 0.802 under 5-fold cross-validation, a 12% and 21% relative improvement over the best single-scale model. A controlled study over 5 foundation models, 5 base classifiers and 3 scales confirms that the gain holds across encoders, with larger improvements observed at smaller scales.

title: Generative artificial intelligence in jazz improvisation: an Actor-Network Theory perspective.
desc: [Frontiers in psychology] Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) plays an increasingly significant role in the artistic creation process. In the domain of highly interactive human-machine composition, GAI is no longer a passive tool but exhibits a certain degree of agency. Based on Actor-Network Theory (ANT), a social science theoretical framework proposed by French sociologist Bruno Latour and other scholars, GAI can be viewed as a non-human subject endowed with the status of an actor. In jazz improvisation, a representative creative activity, the agency of GAI is manifested in the generation of its specific musical works, presenting a contrast to human creation. Furthermore, this process reveals the leading and constraining factors in the actions of GAI, as well as the potential pathways and mutual interactions of its future co-creative development with humans.

title: Residual-Guided Adaptive Tucker Rank Allocation for Parameter-Efficient MCI Conversion Prediction
desc: Allocating limited trainable capacity across convolutional layers is a central challenge in parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) of pretrained three-dimensional (3D) networks. We propose Residual-Guided Adaptive Tucker Rank Allocation, which jointly selects input- and output-channel ranks under a fixed adapter-parameter budget while preserving the spatial kernel modes. To guide rank selection, we learn task-specific proxy updates from downstream training data and approximate them using candidate Tucker rank pairs. A perturbation analysis bounds the output discrepancy between the fixed proxy network and its Tucker approximation in terms of layerwise reconstruction residuals, motivating residual-based allocation. We normalize each squared residual by the corresponding proxy-update energy to compare relative approximation errors across layers. Dynamic programming minimizes their sum under a global budget constraint that accounts for both channel factors and the Tucker core. This yields a globally optimal allocation over the specified candidate rank pairs. We evaluate the method on the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) cohort for predicting conversion from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer's disease within 36 months, using hippocampal segmentation pretraining. Across five random seeds, the proposed method achieves a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.7706, compared with 0.7239 for fixed-ratio Tucker adaptation and 0.7430 for full fine-tuning. The total number of trainable parameters is limited to approximately 0.618 million, accounting for only 1.45% of the full model. Adaptive Tucker rank allocation thus provides an effective approach to parameter-efficient transfer learning in 3D medical imaging.

title: Physics-enhanced deep learning for dual-branch single-pixel vision via highly scattering media.
desc: [Applied optics] Single-pixel imaging (SPI) offers sensitivity for optical sensing, but dynamic scattering media severely degrade the captured 1D bucket signals, causing traditional image reconstruction algorithms to fail and hindering target recognition. To overcome the resulting sim-to-real gap, we propose a physics-enhanced dual-branch digital twin framework for single-pixel vision in highly scattering environments. By algorithmically embedding physical channel degradations-including optical blooming, spatial misalignment, and dynamic turbulence scintillation-into the synthetic training pipeline, the network learns to extract robust, noise-invariant features directly from heavily corrupted measurements. The architecture utilizes a shared encoder that simultaneously drives a semantic classification branch for rapid target recognition and a parallel spatial reconstruction branch for visual validation. Experimental validations in a dynamically turbid underwater testbed demonstrate that the proposed dual-branch model significantly outperforms conventional mathematical methods, e.g., differential ghost imaging and total variation, in structural fidelity and noise suppression. Furthermore, the framework exhibits exceptional compressive sensing efficiency, achieving a peak classification accuracy of 81.2% at a highly compressed sampling ratio of just 19.53%. The system maintains robust semantic recognition even under extreme physical turbulence, where conventionally reconstructed targets are rendered completely unrecognizable. This physics-enhanced deep learning approach provides a highly efficient solution for real-time optical sensing and target identification in dynamically challenging macroscopic channels.

title: When to Stop Asking: Factor Coverage Bias and LLM Determinability Judgments with Underspecified Information in Medicine
desc: Clinical decision-making often begins with underspecified information and requires not only gathering missing information but also knowing when to stop. This calls for judging determinability (whether the available information is sufficient for a decision) by considering whether missing information could change the conclusion, not simply the amount of available decision-relevant information. Reliance on this amount as a cue for determinability, which we term \textit{factor coverage bias}, could undermine the trustworthiness of large language models (LLMs) through premature conclusions or excessive information gathering, such as unnecessary invasive tests. Yet whether LLMs exhibit this bias remains insufficiently studied. To address this gap, we construct a controlled pairwise benchmark in which LLMs identify the determinable case within each determinable--undeterminable pair. We add a decision-relevant factor to either side while keeping each case's determinability unchanged, and similarly add irrelevant text to distinguish this bias from context-length effects. Adding a relevant factor made LLMs more likely to select the augmented case as determinable even when it remained undeterminable, an effect that persisted with increased reasoning effort, while adding irrelevant text made them less likely to select the augmented case, an effect that reasoning substantially reduced. These findings identify factor coverage bias as a failure mode distinct from context-length effects and a potential risk to LLM trustworthiness. Our work provides an evaluation framework for LLM trustworthiness under underspecification.

title: Liquid and solid layers in a thermal deep-learning machine.
desc: [Physical review. E] We study generalization in overparameterized deep neural networks using a thermal deep learning machine with a well-defined Hamiltonian. We find that learning dynamics organize the network into a solid-liquid-solid structure, where boundary layers are constrained while central layers remain flexible. These layers exhibit distinct dynamical behaviors, including timescale separation and nonequilibrium aging. We show that the solution space is structureless in liquid layers but hierarchically organized in solid layers, indicating a direct link between dynamics and landscape geometry. These results suggest a physical perspective for generalization, arising from the interplay between flexible representations and boundary-induced constraints.

title: Reliability-Preserving Compression for Deployable Medical Image Segmentation
desc: Post-training compression of pretrained medical segmentation models commonly uses quantization, pruning, or distillation to reduce model size and computational cost. Existing medical segmentation quantization studies mainly evaluate Dice, model size, memory, and latency, but this is incomplete for safety-critical use because compressed models should also preserve uncertainty signals that indicate unreliable predictions. We study this problem in compressed MRI/CT segmentation and formalize why Dice can remain stable while uncertainty changes. Motivated by this failure mode, we propose score-guided aggregate-validated mixed precision (SGAV-MP), a post-training compression framework that selects layer precisions under reliability constraints. SGAV-MP ranks quantization actions with a compact benefit-risk score and accepts them only after full-model reliability validation on a calibration set. Across five 2D backbones and three 3D benchmarks, SGAV-MP preserves FP32-level Dice and high uncertainty-map agreement, achieving $3.59\times$--$7.8\times$ compression in 2D and $4.73\times$--$7.82\times$ in 3D. We also report backend-supported TensorRT deployment measurements separately to distinguish runtime execution from reliability-preserving storage compression.

title: Mining the Self-Rewriting System: A Vision for Data Mining on AI-Native Infrastructure
desc: Classical data mining treats data as generated outside the learner. Emerging AI-native infrastructure invalidates this assumption: as agents observe system state, act, update retrieval stores and models, and promote new artifacts into the serving path, their own decisions reshape the future logs, traces, corpora, and evaluation records used for later training and release. We call this new research object a self-rewriting system and the resulting system-induced distribution shift endogenous drift. Our central, falsifiable claim is that cross-surface causes are not identifiable in general from marginal per-surface monitoring: different coupled failures can produce the same individual signals while differing in their joint behavior, requiring joint analysis for reliable attribution. This agenda comprises four foundational research problems: fusing heterogeneous drift signals into calibrated gating and attribution (C1); mining agent traces whose activity alphabet evolves (C2); maintaining knowledge fabrics through online reindexing, faithfulness, and compression decisions (C3); and safely promoting concurrent learning streams through one shared evaluation gate (C4). These remain fragmented across concept drift, performative prediction, process mining, streaming retrieval-augmented generation, and MLOps, without a unified data-mining agenda. We outline public benchmarks and evaluation criteria, using AI-native telecom only as a motivating exemplar with analogues in finance, software CI/CD, and clinical decision support.

title: A discrete-continuous-time stochastic framework for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder-related symptom modeling and pharmacological intervention via methylphenidate
desc: This paper presents an original mathematical and computational framework for modeling the efficacy of methylphenidate as an optimal control policy acting on the nonlinear dynamics of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. Neural processes in ADHD are conceptualized as stochastic processes with trajectories that inherently converge towards stable, yet dysfunctional patterns associated with clinical symptoms. The pharmacological intervention is mathematically formalized as an external control signal that reassesses the system's drift and redirects these trajectories towards neurotypical regimes. To bridge these theoretical stochastic models with empirical clinical data, latent representations are inferred using a novel deterministic hybrid deep learning architecture, combining a one-dimensional convolutional neural network and a Vision Transformer, trained on preprocessed functional magnetic resonance imaging data.

title: EEG-Based Classification of Hypnotic Susceptibility Using Two-Dimensional Convolutional Neural Networks
desc: Guided Imagery (GI) is a mind-based relaxation technique widely used in clinical and therapeutic settings. Objectively assessing whether a patient has entered a relaxed state remains a challenge for clinicians. This study investigates electroencephalography (EEG)-based classification of hypnotic susceptibility using two-dimensional Convolutional Neural Networks (2D CNNs) applied to minimally preprocessed signals, without manual feature extraction. Data were collected from 62 male participants (32 Control, 30 Hypno) using a 256-channel dense array amplifier during Guided Imagery or cognitive task conditions. A sliding-window framework evaluated up to 868 independent models across seven anatomically defined brain regions and 124 ten-second time windows. Segment-level random-split screening was followed by Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) cross-validation to obtain subject-independent performance estimates, and an ensemble approach combined predictions across K = 10 windows. The best single-window model achieved accuracy of 0.82 on the random split. Under LOSO, anterior regions generalised better across subjects: the frontal region achieved mean accuracy of 0.646 (AUC: 0.692). An ensemble of K = 10 windows further improved the prefrontal region to mean accuracy of 0.738. The occipital region, dominant in random-split screening, collapsed to near-chance under LOSO, revealing subject-specific EEG fingerprinting rather than genuine group differences. Bandpass filtering and z-score normalisation suffice for competitive EEG classification without manual feature extraction. Anterior cortical regions are identified as the most generalisable neural markers of hypnotic susceptibility.

title: Corpus Quality Improves, Retrieval Utility Does Not: An Ablation of Preprocessing and Refinement in a Speech-to-QA Pipeline
desc: Practitioners building training corpora with a pipeline of language models keep a preprocessing or refinement (post-process) stage when switching it on raises the corpus quality. We ablate a production pipeline that turns conference speech into question-answer pairs. The preprocessing stage rewrites the transcript, and the refinement stage filters the generated pairs. Switching each on and off gives four corpora from the same 40 Korean medical and finance sessions. On the corpus itself, quality rises as the stages switch on. Four LLM judges and six human domain experts rank the four corpora the same way, and the fully refined corpus leads by +0.18 and +0.22 on a 1-5 scale. We then ask whether that gain carries downstream. We supply each corpus to six models at inference and measure retrieval accuracy. The ranking does not hold. Enabling the transcript rewrite lowers retrieval accuracy by 0.061, the only stage effect that survives correction for multiple comparisons. That stage also reads the whole session, so it almost doubles the cost of one. With both stages on, accuracy does not change. An equivalence test we declared in advance confirms this. The corpus itself is clearly valuable. It lifts retrieval accuracy from 0.231 to 0.748 in every model and domain we test. More than a third of its pairs carry knowledge that neither of two frontier models produces on its own. On our data, the null does not come from weak corpora. A rising score on a rubric of this kind did not predict what the corpus holds for a model.

title: Timing-Aware and Interpretable Self-Attention for Event-Based Wearable Task Transition Detection
desc: Task transition detection aims to identify when a person shifts from one task to another, providing a foundation for continuous health monitoring and timely context-aware interventions.
